Question: What would happen to the world's museums if they were forced to return artifacts, specimens and results of research to the countries where the discoveries were unearthed?
Answer: Greek here! Why do you think that such an action would please countries of rich historical backgrounds? The artifacts displayed abroad are our ambassadors there, we want them to be there, can’t expect every foreigner to visit Greece to learn about our heritage! A lot of these artifacts ended up abroad totally legitimate; foreign institutes ask and receive a license to dig and then can take part of the findings; artifacts in excess are sold from the state; there are gifts to foreign museums or prominent persons, etc. Take Nike of Samothrace as an example; the amateur archaeologist Champoiseau asked and received permission to dig and take the findings. Well, he was a lucky guy, he found a masterpiece! As a result, every new finding from the same dig goes to the Louvre, no problem… Is there a problem? Yes! The problem is the smuggled objects. Artifacts that are snitched out of the country, with a practically unknown precise origin. This makes them lose their historical value and even confuse the research, like the Aegina Treasure collection of the British Museum. It is a collection of supposedly Minoan artifacts found on the island of Aegina and were smuggled out of the country; only there are not all of them Minoan….The Aegina Treasure Reconsidered1 | Annual of the British School at Athens | Cambridge Core This is supposed to be a Minoan jewel, but it is not. Researchers spend their time trying to figure out where did it come from, instead of having the information from the excavator…Image from Creative Commons - Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported - CC BY-SA 3.0 It’s smuggling that has to stop, not foreign researchers revealing our past.

Question: Why were the Greeks so advanced? Why is it that some ways they were more advanced than us?
Answer: The Greeks were indeed an advanced civilization of their time and we still admire the Greek statues or the Parthenon. However, their contribution to humanity was neither refined art (many peoples before them created artifacts) nor architecture. What set them apart from their contemporaries was the separation of science from religion. With the weapon of logical thinking and public dialogue, they were able to formulate and deepen concepts, thus laying the foundations of philosophy and science. And something else: although they were not the first to develop writing, they were the first to understand the power of the written word (the earliest examples of Greek writing are from inn customers, not from priests or philosophers). The formation of opinions and concepts through dialogue and their documentation led to the continuous development of science, philosophy, and literature. This is a big step ahead. Why did they do it? I can’t really tell. I think that nobody can! Factors such as the diverged Greek geographical relief or the curiosity of the Greek people played a role but the Phoenicians lived in city-states too, had a writing system, and were tremendously good traders and took a different path. So, let’s enjoy what they offered to us without wondering about the reasons. But we must be realistic when discussing ancient societies, they were not even close to the modern one. 2,000 years of development in science, medicine, and social rights make our era a much better one to live in, despite its serious flaws. No matter how good were the Greeks in philosophy, they could do nothing to reduce the horrible 40% mortality rate of children under 5 years. And how many among us want to work until they die (there was no social security)? We are trained to appreciate a civilization judging from its artifacts but…what about the things that really matter?

Question: What’s a delicious and satisfying meal you recommend for someone who’s really hungry?
Answer: The best combination to satisfy a very hungry person is pasta (because its starch is absorbed the fastest) and a kind of protein (to keep them full for a long). This is a suggestion for a dish from Greek cuisine, giouvetsi. It is a type of protein (usually veal, beef or chicken but you can make it with seafood or even mushrooms) cooked in the same pot with pasta (orzo or chylopites, a type of Greek pasta made from flour, eggs, and milk). It can be made in a casserole or an oven. Veal giouvetsi with orzo and with chylopites seafood giouvetsi and with mushrooms A note: Although it looks like an easy-to-make recipe, it isn’t, a disaster is closer than you think. So, my suggestion is, if you’re not experienced in Greek cuisine, don’t try this at home.

Question: Has the city of Troy been found?
Answer: The usual process to declare YES, a 100% in archaeology is to find an inscription connecting directly the site with the city in question. In Troy, this hadn’t happened yet so, the formal answer is maybe. The famous site has two more major issues; Schliemann’s clumsy excavation has destroyed part of the stratigraphy, depriving the research of valuable elements and the historicity of the Trojan War in Greek mythology doesn’t coincide with the historical information from the Hittite archives. The latter narrates a fuss about a city called Willusa or Turusa (Ilion or Troy), involving a vassal of the Achiyawan king and a king of this city who fled to Hatusha for help and the Hittites restored him to his throne. This is the closest true story we have to the Trojan War, and, as you see, it is quite different! However, hope dies last. The revealed city corresponds with Homer’s description of it and its surroundings. In addition, Troy VIh, the strongest candidate as the Homeric city, was destroyed by an earthquake or enemy attack (or both) around 1250 BCE, the year that both ancient and modern scholars consider the year of the Trojan War. Troy VIh at its peak. Illustration credit: Christian Jegou, Search - Science Photo Library It is followed by Troy VIIa (1250 - 1200/1175 BCE), a relic of its past greatness, representing a period of decline for the city. The revealed evidence shows a hasty and somewhat careless repair and reuse of the citadel fortifications. Many damaged houses are repaired without much care. Something very serious had happened…This city was also destroyed a little later by invasion (~1200–1175 BCE) but it can’t be Homer’s city as it was impoverished. Perhaps it was destroyed by some group of sea raiders, Mycenaeans included. Burnt idol from Troy VIh (Berlin Neues Museum). Image credit: Jona Lendering - Livius Although we may never find whether a layer of this site is the Homeric Troy (if such a city ever existed) we have a good chance to find out if it was Troy of the historical period. Archaeologists are now working on the Greek city of the historical period and the chance of finding an inscription there is pretty good. Let’s hope that we can finally declare the site as Troy 100%. footnotes Geology corresponds with Homers description of ancient Troy Archaeologists unearth palace, agora and city wall in Troy

Question: Did Athens have female warriors?
Answer: No, like all the Greek city-states, Athens didn’t have female warriors. She didn’t exist in real life… There were only some female leaders of the army, like the Macedonian consort queen Euridice III in 318 BCE who led her army against the revolted Olympias, mother of Alexander the Great and Cratesipolis (314–308 BCE), ruler of Corinth and Sikyon who commanded an army and forced cities to submit to her. However, there are two cases in which Greek women went under arms. In 494 BCE, the poet Telesilla organized the old men, slaves, and women of the city to defend it from the attacking Spartans. The Laconians retreated as they couldn’t risk a defeat by women. The story is disputed as while both Plutarch and Pausanias mention the involvement of the women, Herodotus does not. When King Pyrrhus of Epirus attacked Sparta in 272 BCE, Princess Chilonis led the Spartan women to assist in the defense of the city. Sparta didn’t fall.

Question: Those of you who have traveled or lived in Italy, what things do you really like about Italians, and what do you dislike?
Answer: I’ve been to Italy (the Northern part of the country) more than once. The first one was as a tourist but when my son went to study in Turin (my impressions are from this city), I went not as a tourist but as a visitor, and, believe me on this, this is a huge difference. I had to go to public services, ask for thingies in small shops run by old Italian ladies (think of it, how do ask for hobnails in a foreign language you don’t speak?), find the proper tomato sauce for my ragu… It soon turned out that living in Italy is like living in a part of Greece where nobody speaks the language, so, I adapted easily, and made friends with whom I’m still in touch. I liked both them and their delightfully melancholic city (I’m lying, I love them!). The river Po. Image credit: Andreas Bitados What amazed me the most was their garbo, this Italian term describes them the best, it is somehow synonymous with elegance. They know how to dress and move in a unique way that makes them gracious. It’s not about posh garments, it’s about how to wear cheap clothes and make them pop on you. How do they do it? They avoid garments with large brand name prints on them (‘Why should I be a walking advertisement?’). Also, they prefer to shop in the open markets which offer apart from the usual Chinese stuff, clothes from store clearances and, often enough, stolen ones(🤫). And, ALWAYS they wear a scarf! They protect tradition in every way without becoming chauvinistic. You won’t find many foreign products in the market (which won’t bother you, the Italian ones are very good), they become fierce if you 'mess with' their recipes, and they will find the most imaginative ways to use old buildings and objects (the old Torinese hang the city's flag on their balconies and are fans of Torino FC, not the newer but more popular Juventus FC). View of the city from my son’s apartment. The tall building in the back is Mole Antonelliana, one of Turin’s iconic buildings. Image credit: Andreas Bitados They are amazing drivers. It is a delight, for instance, to see grandmothers driving incredibly in the snow (the MotoGP champion is from Turin, coincidence?). These lovely people have only one big disadvantage; they lack self-confidence. They believe they are the worst, filthiest, most useless people on Earth! This is why they are so glad to hear a compliment about their country and, maybe, this is why they have the impressive and not the historically important sites in the tourist guide. Never mind, I found them myself…and I’ll be back, anyway! They also have a minor one, they love to talk! You ask for simple information, like ‘Should I turn left or right?’ and they tell you a full story. Mama mia:) One last thing; whatever you’ve heard about the Italian obsession with watches and shoes…is true!

Question: Are there descriptions of mythological boats with size etc?
Answer: In Greek mythology (this is the one I know!), we meet with two super fascinating, futuristic ships. Look at the ships of the Phaeacians, for instance; the Phaeacians were an ancient people with advanced civilization, and in the Odyssey are the ones that brought Odysseus to Ithaca in one of their ships. The Phaeacian ships were like no other in their time (neither do we have in our time); they could transmit information in the water and steer without needing a captain or a steer to reach their destination. They were also unsinkable, of course! So, according to Homer (Odyssey, book 8. 555–563), when the Phaeacians wanted to travel, they stated the desired destination to the "Steerless ship (Απίδαλος ναυς)" and it tamed the sea and took them to the port of the country they wanted, easy peasy! We don’t have the dimensions or more descriptions of the vessel but who needs them when you know about the gadgets? A modern interpretation of the ship in Corfu. Image from Κέρκυρα: 'Απήδαλος ναυς' - Η ιστορία του πλοίου χωρίς πηδάλιο που ταξιδεύει με το νου τους επισκέπτες [Εικόνες] Another famous ship in Greek mythology is Argo, the ship of Jason (our main source is Argonautica by Apollodorus). The ship was fast and built for travel in the open sea with the assistance of a sail. Apollodorus stated the ship had fifty oars, which permits us to estimate her length at ~28–33m. However, Argo had more capabilities as goddess Athena herself had given a hand in her construction; The prow of the ship was made with a piece of oak from the oracle of Dodona. The oak was able to speak with a human voice and could tell oracles. In other words, Argo had a radar! The prow of Argo to the right, with a branch attached to the stem post. From a coin of Iolkos (4th c. BCE). Question: Weren't women highly valued in ancient Greece?
Answer: Under the term ‘ancient Greece’ are hiding many states in many periods, so, it’s difficult to tell in a nutshell. The ancient Greek societies, even the most progressive among them, were patriarchic, and over-the-top sexist. From their perspective, men’s duty was to become warriors, and women’s duty was to bear future warriors. Since the social and political life was mostly about war, women had limited or even zero place in the affairs of a city. But, did they value and appreciate the mothers of their future protectors? In ancient literature, we read many comments about women, unfortunately almost all of them by male authors, which is a bad start (how many ancient Greek women do you know?). Since we can’t ask the common citizens, let’s search the opinion of the sagas. Hesiod in the Archaic period, writes in Theogony (590–602): …the tender race of women are descended [from Pandora], are a great misfortune for mortals, sharing the homes of men, companions not of cursed poverty, but of abundance. Just as bees feed the drones in their hives, they are partners in evil deeds. Because women, all day long, until the sun sets, run about daily and make the white honeycombs, while the drones stay in the covered hives and gather the toil of others into their own bellies. In the same way, Zeus, who thunders from above, has decreed women as a misfortune for mortal men, are partners in bitter deeds. Not very flattering! In the classic period, things didn’t improve. Menander in a comedy (fragment 702) writes: The man who teaches a woman to write should realize that he is offering poison to a wasp Aristotle in Politics: Between the sexes, the male is by nature superior and the female inferior; the man is the ruler, and the woman is the one being ruled. Even doctors shared the opinion that women were inferior. Soranos (1st century CE) writes in his work About Women (1.16): Therefore, it is not surprising that the woman is more imperfect than the man since she is colder. Just as the mole has imperfect eyes... the woman is more imperfect than the man in her reproductive organs. For the organs were formed within her as she developed in the womb, but they could not develop completely. He thinks that women are amputated men, really now? Let’s face it, women were thought of as inferior and mean and this is not how you value a person. Even in times and states where women had more privileges and esteem (like in Laconia, Macedonia, and Epirus), discrimination against them was present. However, I think that deep down, the Greeks were afraid of women. Read what Euripides write in Hippolytos: It goes without saying that a woman is a great evil: the parent gives birth to her, raises her, and then gives a dowry to get rid of her, to be free of her. And the man who takes her in brings bad seed into his home, adorns her beautifully to enjoy her, spending all his wealth, poor soul. Better to have a foolish woman, who cannot cause harm due to her lack of sense. I hate the clever ones! I don't want them in my house, especially if they have too much intelligence. In their minds, Aphrodite plants the most wicked schemes. But the foolish ones, with their limited minds, don't cause trouble. What do you think of it?

Question: Byzantine adopted Roman construction methods in some aspects, however it differs. How does their construction method differ from that of the Roman construction method?
Answer: The ‘Byzantines’ were in fact Romans so, they didn’t adopt but rather developed the construction methods in some cases. For instance, as Christianity became the dominant religion of the Roman Empire, a new type of temple was needed. The pagan temples were replaced by the basilicas of the early years which transformed gradually into the great Byzantine order churches. The Byzantine Empire kept city planning, the agora, and the use of public monuments such as statues of important figures and monumental arches and city gates from the earlier periods. Fortifications, bridges, public baths, hippodromes, and cisterns were still constructed but other public constructions like theaters, stadiums, and gymnasia fell out of use as the church didn’t approve of them. The Byzantines employed bricks as the basic element of construction. A little bigger than Roman bricks, were square and measured up to 38 cm (15 inches) along each side with a height of up to 6.5 cm (2.5 inches). Bricks were used to create walls by laying two faces and pouring rubble and mortar between them. The mortar was made from lime, sand, and crushed brick or pebbles. Every so often a strengthening layer made wholly of bricks runs through the entire wall. Unlike Roman, the Byzantine version did not use a concrete (pozzolana) core, and so if the facing became damaged, then, eventually, so too did the core. See what I mean in the image below (Towers of the Land Walls of Constantinople). image from Walls & Fortifications They also used a much thicker layer of mortar between bricks, probably as a cost-saving exercise as fewer bricks were needed. This came with a cost; as the mortar dried, it warped, and many buildings suffered from distortion or even partial collapse. Bricks were also used for domes, arches, and vaults, often employing bricks double the standard size. An alternative to brick was ashlar stone blocks, which were more popular in the Empire’s eastern half, like this androne from Sergilla, Syria. Byzantine Dead Towns - Sergilla Marble was generally reserved for columns, capitals, cornices, architraves, and decorative features such as door frames, window grills, and paving. It was often a ‘donation’ from older constructions in disuse, like temples. The eclectic mix of columns and capitals within the same structure eventually became a mark of Byzantine buildings. However, the greatest contribution of Byzantine architecture is the dome. True, the dome predated the Byzantine Romans, everybody still admires the impressive dome of the Pantheon in Rome. But the Byzantine ones, which represent heaven, stand on supporting pendentives (spherical triangles, forming the transition from the circular plan of the dome to the polygonal plan of its supporting structure), thus, they can be huge (Aghia Sophia’s dome is 184 ft tall). from Image of Aghia Sophia’s dome from Hagia Sophia and Basilica Cistern with Combo Ticket » Hagia Sophia The development of the dome created a new style, especially in the construction of religious buildings which influenced both the Islamic and Western architecture. Here are two excellent examples: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International San Marco in Venice. Question: What are the misconceptions between speed and velocity?
Answer: Speed and velocity are synonyms except for when used in physics. In a scientific text, speed describes how fast an object moves. It is a scalar quantity; we only care about the amount (30km/h, 100m/s, or any other speed unit). However, velocity is something different. It is a vector that informs us not only on how fast an object is moving but also in which direction. We graph velocity (which is why it can be troublesome). This means that an object can have a constant speed but a changing velocity if, for example, it is moving in a circular path. The object is moving at the same speed but the velocity in the ‘South’ is opposite to that of the ‘North’. This is also why when we refer to the famous c, we always call it the speed of light because it doesn’t matter whether the light source is moving toward or away from us, we always get the same measurement (speed) of light.

Question: Where does the Athenian Parthenon Temple get its name?
Answer: We don’t know! But, there are some theories about it; a. Parthenon may mean ‘the temple of the virgin goddess’ as Athena was one of the virgin (another term with unclear meaning) goddesses. There is an issue in this one as the adjective virgin was mainly used for Artemis, not Athena, who was named Polias or Pallas. b. It was named after a room located in the west cella of the temple. Some scholars argue that it was the place where the sacred veil was worn on the statue of Athena by the Arrephores, a group of four virgin girls chosen to serve their city each year during the Panathenaia. Do you see the small room in the back of the temple? That was the girls’ room. Other scholars claim that they resided in the Erechtheion. Image from Πώς σώθηκε ο Παρθενώνας το 1821 c. The term may be a reference to the virgin daughters of King Cecrops who sacrificed their lives to save the city. We don’t know when the temple was named Parthenon either. The architects Iktinos and Kallikratis (5th century) seem to have referred to the building as "Hekatompedos" (Cathedral) in their lost treatise on Athenian architecture, and during the 4th century onwards, the building was referred to as "Hekatompedos" or "Hekatompedon" as well as "Parthenon". The first source in which the temple is characterized as the Parthenon is a text by the orator Demosthenes in the 4th century BCE. Plutarch (1st century CE) referred to the temple as "Hekatompedos Parthenon". Note: The notion that the Parthenon was named as such during the Christian period is wrong, the Christian temple was dedicated to Panaghia Atheniotissa (Holy Mary of Athens).

Question: Why aren’t Olympic gold medals pure gold anymore?
Answer: The winners’ Olympic medal was pure gold only in three Olympiads, in Saint Luis (1904), in London (1908), and in Stockholm (1912) as until then there were no specifications about the award. For instance, in the first Olympiad in Athens, the winners’ medals were made of silver and in Paris (1900) cups were awarded. Question: How is the speed of gravity determined?
Answer: The speed of gravitational waves would be a more proper expression. They are 'ripples' in space-time with the strongest (thus measurable) of them caused by some of the most violent and energetic processes in the Universe, like the colliding of black holes and neutron stars, supernovae, etc. Image: Shutterstock According to the Newtonian model, gravity propagates instantaneously: the force exerted by a massive object points directly toward that object's present position. For example, even though the Sun is 500 light seconds from Earth, Newtonian gravity describes a force on Earth directed towards the Sun's position "now," not its position 500 seconds ago. Wrong description! The theory of general relativity predicts that the speed of gravitational waves exactly equals the speed of light in the vacuum, as all massless particles travel at this speed. The theoretical prediction that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum has been confirmed experimentally. LIGO has been directly detecting gravitational waves since 2015 and various groups have been directly detecting bursts of gamma ray light since 1967. A particular neutron star merger event in the NGC 4993 galaxy created both a burst of gamma-ray light and chirped gravitational waves at almost exactly the same time. They then reached Earth’s LIGO ( Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory) and gamma-ray detectors almost simultaneously., proving that the speed of light and the speed of gravity are the same, out to the fifteenth digit.

Question: How and why was wine and opium (found in remnants) of ancient Canaanite graves in the Jezreel Valley used?
Answer: Jezreel or Megiddo Valley is a fertile plain in Northern Israel, the ‘breadbasket’ of the country today. In history, the region is mostly known for the battle between Egyptian and Hittite troops back in the Bronze Age and it is from back then that changed rulers continually. File:WV Jezreel Valley region and mount Gilboa in Israel.png - Wikimedia Commons The vessels that contained the opium date back to the 14th century BCE(Late Bronze Age), and they were found in Canaanite graves, apparently having been used in local burial rituals. It is the earliest known evidence of its use although the hallucinogenic drug is referred to Sumerian clay tablets written in Cuneiform script c. 3000 BCE. The Egyptians also cultivated it and was used by priests, magicians, and warriors, and was associated with religious cultism. The opium in the graves was found in jugs and juglets carefully sealed, and uncontaminated (this is why the accurate chemical analysis was possible) along with vessels containing wine, beeswax, and vanilla(!) of unknown origin. One of the jars found at Horvat Tevet, in northern Israel. (courtesy Omer Sergi) During the Late Bronze Age, the religious and social structure in Canaan changed and became more heterogeneous compared to the Canaanite society of the Middle Bronze Age. After the fall of the Hyksos fortresses in the Delta region of the Nile, there was an invasion by the pharaohs of Egypt into the Levant during the reign of pharaohs Amenhotep I and Thutmose III (18th dynasty). Subsequently, the southern Levant was largely subject to Egyptian political control that greatly influenced Canaanite culture and religion. The archeological finds from tombs and temples show that the Canaanites in this period were influenced by the cultures of Egypt, Middle Syria, the Hittite kingdom, Cyprus, and the Aegean islands. Archaeological evidence shows that the community took care to keep burials and skeletons intact. Concern over the integrity of human remains at the sites indicates the diffusion into the Canaanite religion of the Egyptian belief that the soul or the spirit, which left the body at the moment of death, would return to it. The opium probably had to play a role in this although specific details are not documented. Question: Was Cyrus the Great killed or did he die naturally?
Answer: Cyrus II The Great, also known to the Greeks as Cyrus the Elder, (~600-530 BCE) was the founder of the Persian Empire. Starting from the Iranian plateau, this magnificent, innovative leader managed to conquer all the lands between Iran and the Mediterranean Sea. However, Cyrus was also unlucky. The Persians didn’t write down their history so, all we know about him, apart from some inscriptions, are from other peoples’ writings (mainly from the Greeks and the Hebrews). Their information is frequently vague and contradictory and the conditions of his death are no exception. Encyclopaedia Iranica has a good sum-up of what we know: In 530 BCE Cyrus mounted a campaign to Central Asia to protect the north­eastern borders of his empire from incursions by the Massagetae. During a battle along the lower Oxus (Āmū Daryā) near the Aral Sea the emperor was not only defeated but also killed. His death has been dated to July or August (Parker and Dubberstein, p. 14), but a recently published document from Kish in Babylonia is dated the 19th day of the month Arahsamna in the ninth regnal year of Cyrus, that is, 4 December 530 BCE (McEwan, no. 123). It therefore appears that the battle must have taken place at the very end of 530. Conflicting legends about Cyrus’ death have been transmitted. The Greek authors reported that he lost 200,000 men in the battle with the Massagetae, an obvious exaggeration. A particularly popular version was recounted at length by Herodotus, who also noted that many other accounts were in circulation (Herodotus, 1.201-14). According to this version, followed by variations by other classical authors, Cyrus attacked one camp of the Massagetae, but their main forces subsequently defeated his forces and killed him. According to Berossus, Cyrus died in a battle with the Daai (Dahae, Burstein, p. 29), whereas Ctesias claimed that Cyrus’ last campaign was fought against the Derbici, a Central Asian tribe, who were assisted by Indian troops. Supposedly it was an Indian spear that wounded Cyrus, who died several days later (König, p. 4 no. 6). According to Xenophon, Cyrus died peacefully in his own capital, having ordered that his corpse be buried in the earth, rather than encased in silver or gold (Cyropaedia 8.7.25); some scholars believe that this version is rooted in Persian tradition (e.g., Hirsch, p. 84). Herodotus and other Greek authors also relied on Persian oral tradition, however. Although it is not possible now to discern the precise facts of Cyrus’ death (Sancisi-Weerdenburg, p. 471), it is known that he was buried at Pasargadae (now Mašhad-e Morḡāb). This fact appears to belie the details reported by Herodotus, but it is possible that Cyrus’ body was recovered from the enemy and brought to the capital; Ctesias maintained that Cambyses sent a certain Bagapates to accompany the corpse of Cyrus to the funeral (König, p. 5, no. 9). Cyrus the Great tomb. It is a gabled funerary chamber of six-stepped courses made of large sandstone blocks. The chamber is entered through a low, narrow doorway. Arrian (Anabasis 6.29.4-11) and Strabo (15.3.7) based their descriptions of this chamber on reports by the compan­ions of Alexander the Great, who had visited it personally. It contained Cyrus’ golden coffin and a couch covered with hides dyed purple, on which the royal garments, bracelets, daggers, and other attributes were placed. They had, however, already been plun­dered when Alexander made his second visit to Pasargadae. Since the early Islamic period, the tomb of Cyrus has been known as Mašhad-e Mādar-e Solaymān (the tomb of the mother of Solomon). The only documented thing about Cyrus’ death is that he died…

Question: Why do rainbows always have the shape of half circle & full circle rather than other fractions of a circle? Equating a rainbow to sine waves, what is a negative rainbow?

Image credit: Rainbow at the end of 2015 Tucson AZ monsoon season A rainbow is a collection of rays from glinting raindrops that happen to reach our eyes. Raindrops glint rainbow rays at an angle of 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the sun. All the drops glinting in the rainbow are on the surface of a cone with its point at your eye. Other drops not on the cone also glint sunlight into rainbow colors but their rays do not reach our eyes. We only see those on the cone. When you look down the cone you see a circle. So rainbows are circles! from EPOD - a service of USRA . It was realized by Rene Descartes in the 1600s that a primary rainbow is a complete circle with a radius of approximately 42 degrees -- the minimum deviation angle of sunlight passing through raindrops. Question: Why is the island of Samothrace associated with mythology and cults?
Answer: Samothrace is an island like no other in the Aegean. It is mountainy (mount Saos counts 1,600m, making it the highest mountain on an island), with wild, virgin forests, and plenty of water. It’s literally a mountain surrounded by the sea, nothing like the barren islands of the Cyclades or the nearby Lemnos. Samothrace is a wild landscape, with fierce winds that make the Cycladic ones seem like a gentle breeze, and snow in the winter, with gorges and cliffs, rivers that often drown people when they overflow (the largest one is called Fonias=Killer for a reason). Saos welcomes you as you approach the shore. The locals call it the Moon because it hides the moon… The lowest lake and waterfall of Fonias, the only one with easy access (one-hour hiking). There are six more higher on the slope. People have lived there since pre-history before the arrival of the Greeks. You see, despite the difficulties of everyday life on the island (even today), Samothrace has a big advantage, it provides safety. It has no good ports and people could easily find shelter in the mountains in invasions. In short, people went there to hide and they are still hiding. Travelers are not welcome (I can narrate countless stories on this…) in Samothrace, the locals keep the biggest distance possible. So, it is not a surprise that these isolated islanders developed a mystic cult, the Kabeiria. In the sanctuary of the Great Gods, the "Great Gods" or "Gods" are never referred to as Kabeiri, evil spirits, evil demons who from the depths of the earth and the bottom of their mother of the sea exploded fire and shook the earth. Earthquakes and fires were attributed to them. They were also short in height, had large genitals, and were supernatural spirits representing underground fire and mining operations. (Do they remind you of some other entities?) We know the names of some of their gods; Axieros (the Greeks identify him as Hades), Axiocersa (Demeter for the Greeks), Cadmilos (Hermes). According to their founding (Greek) legend of the sanctuary in Samothrace, the goddess Demeter fell in love with a mortal, Hetion, who knew about the Kabeirian mysteries. This relationship with the mortal annoyed Zeus, as a result of which he killed the young man. Later, Zeus regretted it and decided to build the sanctuary himself, to ease Demeter's pain. Thus, he chose this temple to be towards the Kabeiri, since Hetion had been initiated into these mysteries. Do you get what those people were trying to do? They tried to get in touch with the wild nature around them and appease it in every possible way. They still do it annually during the Carnival, a completely pagan ritual. Samothrace is worth a visit for sure (it’s a must, IMO). Don’t expect to find the usual welcome spirit of the touristy islands, it isn’t there. You’ll feel the power of nature instead, ever-present in every corner of the place. A priceless feeling…

Question: What caused the Greek Dark Age?
Answer: It was the Bronze Age collapse. The collapse in the Aegean region was completed by the end of the 12th century BCE, leaving the Greek peninsula with the administration centers ruined and semi-abandoned. Many members of the nobility and the loyal craftsmen had fled to start a new life in other places, archaeologists have found many of those ‘shelters’ all over the Mediterranean. A part of the remaining population established new, shabby settlements in mountainy locations. The place was left without administration and leadership, it was total chaos and nothing could go worse…only it did! The horrendous drought going on for the last two centuries before the collapse (it was one of its causes) went on for two centuries more resulting in a severe decrease in the population (estimations vary between 40% and 90(!)%). The only sparkles of hope in this dystopia were a few cities (Athens, Miletus, Lefkandi, and Chalkis in Euboia) which were left intact, and step-by-step, a new civilization emerged three or four centuries later. The period between the collapse and the rise of the Greek civilization is called the Greek Dark Age, mainly due to the lack of a writing system. However, the Dark Age wasn’t a period in which nothing happened; the burial customs changed (the Early Helladic ones returned), the architecture changed (different houses, temples replaced the megaron, and palaces ceased to exist), and the social and political system changed too. Reconstruction of Proto-Geometric houses, nothing like the two-story Mycenaean ones. New technologies did find their way to Greece (iron processing, the mines in Laurion were put in operation again, new better wheel in pottery). After the adaptation of the Phoenician alphabet (the earliest inscriptions are dated in the 8th century but scholars believe writing arrived earlier), the progress was exponential, and..you know the rest…

Question: Why is there no evidence of a multiverse theory?
Answer: There is more than one theory (actually, they are hypotheses) about the multiverse. There are so many that the cosmologist Max Tegmark categorized them into four levels and… this is a bad start because this means that none of them is complete. At level 1, the other universes are extensions of our universe, with the same physical constants and the same physical laws. They are areas that are moving away from us so quickly that their light will never be able to reach us, no matter how much time passes. At level 2, we come across a quite different interpretation of the Multiverse, we have independent universes – bubbles that all arose through the same mechanism and have the same or different physical constants.. According to the theory of inflation, space inherently contains energy, which leads to the rapid expansion of space itself and the appearance of particles, i.e. matter and energy. Schematically, we could say that each universe is like a bubble in the same lake. These bubbles are separated from birth and each follows its own evolutionary path. At level 3, we find the parallel universes of the interpretation of the many worlds of Quantum Mechanics. Each quantum possibility corresponds to another universe. (Image: Scientific American) In Quantum mechanics, the position and behavior of a particle are described by a wave function, that is, by a relationship that gives us the probability that the particle is in a certain region. As long as we do not interact with them, the resulting picture is what they behave as waves. Conversely, when we observe them, that is, we interact with them they are treated as simple particles. The most popular and accepted interpretation of this strange phenomenon is the Copenhagen interpretation. According to it, the Universe is inherently probabilistic and, in essence, at the moment of observation the wave function collapses. That is, the position of the particle takes a specific value based on probabilities. Everett's interpretation of the multiverse doesn’t accept the collapse of the wave function. According to it, there is a universe for every possible quantum state. That is, infinite universes are created each time a particle is observed. Finally, at level 4, all universes that can be described mathematically are included. The criticism of the Multiverse hypothesis (but also of theories such as string theory) is that while they are products of mathematical logical reasoning, they seem to be unfalsifiable. That is, they cannot be debunked or proven experimentally. In other words, they don’t fulfill the fundamental law of science… footnotes Max Tegmark's excellent article in Scientific American which I recommend you study: https://space.mit.edu/home/tegmark/PDF/multiverse_sciam.pdf

Question: Was the Minoan Civilization a unified state, or a collection of city-states?
Answer: Despite the popular notion that the Minoans were an ever-thriving, powerful kingdom, the archaeological indications show that they had a lot of ups and downs and changes in the 2,000 (note, it’s two millennia!) years of their history. Here’s a brief timeline of their (political) works and days: In the pre-Palatial period (~2600–1900 BCE), the Minoans were hardly organized, no palaces were still built but the evidence shows that there were at least four different clans on the island. In the proto-Palatial period (1900–1700 BCE), the islanders were organized into four states (probably kingdoms), the administration was present and the first hieroglyphic writing appeared. The differences between the architectural structure of the palatial centers and the pottery styles, the guards on the roads, and the different burial customs as well, make the historians believe that the states were more than one (actually four). Plan of Phaistos, Protopalatial period, showing typical characteristics of this period (open central court, storage spaces, and elite domestic spaces). Image from https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/ancient-art-civilizations/aegean-art1/minoan/a/minoan-art-introduction In the Neo-Palatial period (1700–1450 BCE) after a period that seemed marked by riots or civil wars (or maybe a natural disaster), the four states finally unified, at least, this is what the uniformity in architecture and customs imply. The Neo-Palatial Center at Knossos. Image from Palace of Knossos - Hidden Architecture Around 1450 BCE, the island of Crete was subjugated by the Mycenaeans. During the Bronze Age collapse, the Mycenaean regime perished and Crete followed them down. However, the beautiful frescoes you admire at Knossos are from the post-Palatial (Mycenaean) period… Later, in the historical period, the Cretans were organized into city-states like the rest of the Greeks. The fierce rivalry between the two main cities, Knossos in the northwest and Lissos in the southeast makes me believe that the old rivalry between the Cretan regions was never forgotten… PS. Knossos won!

Question: What are the spiritual implications of quantum physics?
Answer: Quantum physics, although a shocking theory, has nothing to do with spirituality but with natural philosophy instead. It dissolves the causality of classical physics (not classical physics itself; the two are completely compatible) and defines the universe as inherently probabilistic. Yes, God does play dice. To make matters worse, probability in this context does not have the same meaning as in everyday life. When we say that if we flip a coin it will land heads or tails, it means that we do not have all the information needed to make an absolutely accurate prediction (such as the angle of the toss, the initial speed, possible hand tremors, etc.). If we knew all these factors, we could accurately predict which side the coin would land on. However, in quantum physics, all probabilities have values even if we know all the parameters. In other words, God not only plays dice but He cheats also! How does quantum physics do this? With its fundamental principle, namely the dual nature of matter that can be simultaneously particles and waves. This has consequences with the most important of them being Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, which explains that we cannot simultaneously know the position and the velocity of a particle/wave (you can easily understand this, a wave does not occupy ONLY ONE point...). It is difficult for humans to reconcile with this paradoxical physics that tells us, for example, that an electron can overcome energy barriers greater than the energy it possesses (it's like saying a person can pass through a wall). However, it is not impossible when one considers that quantum physics effortlessly answers all the questions that classical physics "gets stuck" on. For example, according to classical physics, electrons should fall into the nucleus of atoms (and they don't). In short, quantum physics is a (very successful) suggestion on how the world works and has nothing to do with spirituality and mysticism. How does it come in the era of the supposed triumph of science the most successful scientific theory of all time—quantum mechanics—is being used today as the prime tool for manipulating and deceiving people around the world under the banner of the so-called New Age and the Eastern mysticism that accompanies it? Moreover, this "industry" is actively supported by a growing number of university professors in the USA and beyond. We can have our answer if we think that, while the scientific revolution of the 17th century led to the Enlightenment, the abolition of "divine right" regimes, and ultimately the establishment of democratic governments, the scientific revolution of the early 20th century now faces a swelling wave of hostility against the very spirit of science. This is a deep hostility similar in nature to that of the Catholic Church towards everything Galileo represented—the reliance on experience and reason as the only valid source of knowledge about the natural world. Is it a coincidence that this intellectual hostility towards fundamental science and the Enlightenment, which is currently on the rise in democratic countries—and the mass appeal of irrationality and pseudoscience—has striking similarities to the phenomena that dominated interwar Germany? Fundamental science flourished—according to science historian Thomas Kuhn—"only in cultures that derive from ancient Greece". That is, only in cultures that embraced the challenge of democracy and carried it forward to this day. And if indeed science and democracy always go hand in hand, could it be that hostility towards science—not towards its technological applications, but towards the very spirit of science, its radical anti-dogmatism—has always been a bad omen for the future of democracy itself? Think of it, please, and don’t be afraid of true science…

Question: Is it true that we found Dyson Spheres in our Galaxy?
Answer: A Dyson sphere is a hypothetical construction of an advanced alien civilization that permits them to exploit all the energy of their solar system (that is their star). It was proposed in the 1960s by physicist Freeman Dyson (he “borrowed” the idea from a sci-fi novel!) and it’s about enormous shells that wrap around stars, absorbing as much light energy as possible. The material used to construct these spheres would come from disassembled planets in that star's system. But no energy collection or usage system is perfect. So, while the Dyson sphere collects radiation from the star on its inside, it also emits heat from its outside. To us, that would make a Dyson sphere appear as a star with a lot more infrared radiation than normal and it’ll be a way to detect the alien civilization that constructed it. This is why Dyson suggested the theory in the first place. In the latest search, astronomers identified seven stars in the Milky Way (within 1,000 light-years of Earth) that emit an abnormally large amount of infrared radiation, making them Dyson sphere candidates. Hot, dust-obscured galaxies (Hot DOGs), like the one circled in purple, may have similar energy signatures to hypothetical alien structures called Dyson spheres, new research suggests. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA) A more recent study excluded three of them as a rare kind of galaxy known as Hot DOGs (Hot DOGs are surrounded by enormous, thick clouds of dust, and warm dust is very good at emitting infrared radiation). The other four may also be Hot DOGs because of the similarities in the various wavelengths of light emitted by all seven candidates but they are still under investigation. Stay tuned… for more details

Question: Was the Trojan War fake or true?
Answer: We used to know about the Trojan War from ancient Greek poems and tragedies, such as the Iliad, the Odyssey (there is a more detailed description of the events in it), the Atreids trilogy of Sophocles, and commentaries of later authors. The common belief was it was a fascinating myth and nothing more although for the ancient Greeks was a true event. And then, Schliemann unearthed a Bronze Age city that has a lot of characteristics of the Homeric Troy and the quest for the reveal of the Trojan War caught on fire. The archaeological findings didn’t help much as Schliemann’s amateurish work had destroyed possible evidence but as Deus ex Machina, the Hittite archives came to shed light on an invasion that happened in the 13th c. BCE, that is, matches with the estimated date of the legendary war. However, the historical, true events are completely different! A summary of what the archives narrate: First of all, meet Piyama-Radu, a Luwian nobleman without a kingdom who all his life fought desperately to acquire one, preferably in Western Anatolia. He created great problems with his actions among his contemporary Hittite Great Kings. Such was his troublesome presence that the Hittites used not only their strong military power but also diplomacy and even magic to neutralize him. Piyama-Radu had excellent relations with the Mycenaeans to whom he remained a loyal vassal to the end, acting as a representative of the Mycenaean king and probably spent a large part of his life in the Mycenaean territory. During the reign of Muwattalli II, he invaded the Seha River Land and humbled its vassal king Manapa-Tarhunta with a crushing military defeat, capturing his kingdom. Muwattalli II took action and sent a strong Hittite expeditionary force to the region, which succeeded in recovering the kingdom of Seha River Land with the support of Manapa-Tarhunta, who was restored to his throne. The Hittite texts state that the Hittite expeditionary force moved towards Wilusa (Troy) after the capture of the Seha River Land, without the participation of Manapa-Tarhunta, where it is implied that either a local rebellion had broken out, or the town had been attacked by some external enemy. The participation of the king of Ahhiyawa and Piyama-Radu in these events must be taken for granted. The Hittite army accomplished its mission at Wilusa, defeated the invaders, and restored King Alaksandu to the throne. And this is the closest story to the Trojan War we have so far. Few true elements are included in the myths. The names of Piyama-Radu and Alaksandu were hellenized as Priam and Alexandros (Paris) although their part in the story is completely changed. The most important, the Mycenaeans had lost the war! So, what can we say about the Trojan War, was it real or not? Let’s say it’s another myth with some true elements in its core. The defeat must have cost a lot to the Mycenaeans. Maybe, looking for reality in myths is not a good strategy. Using history to understand the myths seems a better choice… footnotes

Question: Why do you think the Antikythera mechanism doesn't show up in any historical writings?
Answer: As you can imagine…I don’t know and I can’t document anything of what I’m gonna write. However, I have some thoughts on the matter. Scientists write down the new things found, they did so too back in ancient times. Maybe, the inventor of the mechanism did write about it and his book or any other authors’ comments on it are not among the disappointing few surviving technical texts of antiquity. An alternative possibility is no one ever wrote about it because it didn’t add something new to science although its task was innovative. For us, it is a unique device that proved the ancient Greeks knew how to construct small gears (our notion was they constructed only big ones for watermills), had better astronomical and mathematical knowledge than we thought, and had conceived the idea of a computer. We don’t know its use; it seems to be an educational device for training science students in astronomy. We do know it had an ancestor, Archimedes’ planetarium, a device described briefly (and probably not accurately) by Cicero, and a successor, a Byzantine complex geared sundial calendar that proves the continuity in science. However, none of them functioned like the mechanism. It was a device that calculated the dates of religious games such as the Olympic games (future or previous) and the positions of certain celestial bodies on a selected date (future or previous). They put in the data (data!) and it calculated the result. It was nothing less than an analog computer. A possible reconstruction of Archimedes’ planetarium. It was a geared device that showed the daily motion of the stars around the Earth, the eclipses of the Sun and Moon and their movement along the ecliptic, all visible inside a glass sphere representing the universe. Question: What is the best guess as to the sources of the copper and tin that ushered the Egyptians, Mycenaeans, and Minoans into the Bronze Age?
Answer: We have some solid answers on the topic so far. Bronze was produced by the mid-third millennium BCE, the first great period of international contact, with copper and tin being the metals needed for the alloy. The best way to study the origin of the metals is to study ingots. Ingots are a primary form in which copper (tin too) was cast for shipment and therefore a single ingot was probably made from the ores of a single mine. There should be no confusion in ore sources as it happens in the case of artifacts, many of which were fabricated with varying amounts of scrap metal. The wide distribution of ingots too is significant; they are found in Israel, Cyprus, Turkey, Crete, Greece, Sicily, and Sardinia. So, ingots say that our best guess is Alashiya (Cyprus). Cyprus extensively exploited its large deposits of copper which is also well documented by the presence of imple­ments and slags for the ores at Apliki, Enkomi, Athienou, and Kition, and its history pushed back to the Early Bronze Age based on finds at Ambelikou. Cypriot copper was exported to Egypt, Syria, and elsewhere. Cypriot copper ingot (1450–1050 BCE) Copper ingot | Cypriot | Late Bronze Age | The Metropolitan Museum of Art However, Cyprus was not the only copper producer and exporter. Ingots from the Gelidonya and Kyme shipwrecks and four Minoan sites showed a different source of top-quality copper, unfortunately still undetermined. In addition, later results suggest that for Late Bronze Age Crete the Laurion region in Attica, Greece, may have been a more important copper source than Cyprus. If we add the mines in the Aegean islands and Anatolia, we understand that copper was relatively in abundance in the Eastern Mediterranean region. Map showing the major sources of copper and tin in the Bronze Age Europe. Copper deposits are marked with yellow stripes while sources of tin are marked with silver. Tin, on the other hand, is missing. There isn’t any, apart from a mine at Kestel on the outskirts of Nigde, in the Taurus Mountains of south-central Turkey which was abandoned approx. 1800 BCE. So, all the tin ended in the Mediterranean was imported mostly from distant Afghanistan and as has been recently documented from south-west England. The chemical examination of tin ingots found in shipwrecks off the coast of Israel left no doubt. The arrow does not indicate the actual trade route but merely illustrates the assumed origin of the Israeli tin based on the data The case is not closed though. The trade routes, the merchants involved, and possibly more sources of raw metals may be waiting out there to be revealed.. footnotes Bronze age tin from Israeli shipwrecks was mined in Britain Expedition Magazine | Ingots and the Bronze Age Copper Trade in the Mediterranean A New Approach on JSTOR

Question: Photon has no mass, so how does quantum mechanics calculate the momentum of a photon?
Answer: Photon has properties analogous to those of particles we can even see as it interacts as a unit in collisions or when absorbed, rather than as an extensive wave. It is now a well-established fact that photons do have momentum although a very small one. In fact, photon momentum is suggested by the photoelectric effect, where photons knock electrons out of a substance. The relationship between photon momentum p and photon energy E is: E^2=(pc)^2+(mc)^2 Since the photon has no mass, the equation above becomes E=pc or p=E/c (1). The energy of a photon determined from the Plank-Einstein equation is E=hc/λ (2), where h is Plank’s constant and λ is the wavelength of the photon. Combining the relationships (1) and (2) we get p=h/λ. PS. If you calculate the momentum of a photon, you’ll come up with a very small quantity. Compton, the first to observe the effects of photon momentum was observing x-rays, which have a small wavelength and a relatively large momentum, interacting with the lightest of particles, the electron.

Question: Could the Ancient Greeks have gone through an industrial revolution? If so, why didn't they?
Answer: Maybe. Although for centuries the Greeks neither felt the need for automatization (low-cost slaves did the job for them) nor had the means, they had a vision of automata, the Greek myths are loaded with stories about robots. Look what Aristotle, a great supporter of slavery wrote in Politics, Book I: “if every tool, when summoned, or even by intelligent anticipation, could do the work that befits it, just as the creations of Daedalus moved of themselves, or the tripods of Hephaestus went of their own accord to their sacred work, if the weavers’ shuttles were to weave of themselves, then there would be no need either of apprentices for the master craftsmen, or of slaves for the lords.” So, the thought (just the thought) was there. And during the Hellenistic period, when the rise of science was exponential, some automatons started to appear: Hero of Alexandria described hydraulic systems, fire engines, wind-operated machines, and even a self-propelled cart in his book On Automaton-Making, to refer to the most known of them. Still, they used this machinery as toys or to impress visitors of palaces and temples, the thought of industry didn’t occur to them. Hero’s wash basin automaton. It featured metal birds that sang. A mechanical owl would turn its head to look at the birds, making them go quiet. Image from Automata in Greek mythology - The Mechanical Art & Design Museum If they had the opportunity to continue research, maybe, they could reach closer to it. They didn’t. As the Hellenistic kingdoms were under the Roman threat, the financial support to Museums (what we call universities today) stopped and the Romans weren’t exactly research-lovers… Anyway, the industrial revolution requires more than creative designs. More precise tools, better metal alloys, and better measurement tools are also needed. Most importantly, a different mentality was needed and they didn’t have it. They were satisfied using slaves for everything.

Question: How did ancient Greeks entertain themselves?
Answer: The Greeks (ancient and modern) are extrovert people, they like to share their moments with others. So, although in antiquity life was hard and most of the day was spent at work (don’t forget that most of them were farmers), dinner with friends (a quite common custom) was a good opportunity to relax and get rid of the stress of the day. Don’t think of the fancy symposia of the wealthy people, there were more like two or more friends (men only!) sharing their food, sipping their wine, and chatting about everything. At the same time, the women would stay in separate rooms and…do the same! In the big urban centers like Athens or Corinth, the unofficial dinners could be more lavish, a banquet. It can include philosophical discussions, dancing, and singing by professional artists who may offer more private entertainment too (that would be a symposium). Or they could also play games with kottabos being the most popular. The purpose of this game was to achieve a goal. As a shot, they used wine that was hurled with the mouth or thrown by hand holding a shallow plate. The target was the scale, a platter attached high to a stick, or floating in a basin of water. Representation of a kottavos scene on an ancient Greek vase. The balance is mounted on a long stick, while the player aims while holding a disc. Attribution 2.5 Generic However, the biggest opportunity for common people to have fun was at the religious festivities. They would dress in their best clothes, and attempt ceremonies, parades, possibly theatrical performances or/and athletic games. They would dance, sing, flirt (legally or not). And…when think of religious festivities, don’t think only of the Olympic Games and the Panathenaea, there were a lot of religious festivities of local or Panhellenic importance…. The spectacular procession of the horsemen in Panathenaea on Parthenon’s frieze. The real event must be quite a spectacle. : http://my-favourite-planet.de/english/europe/greece/attica/athens/acropolis/acropolis-photos-01-015.htm What else could they do to have fun? They played! Games like the chalki myia (mole fly), akininda (statuettes), pentelitha (pentovola), and more that the Greeks among you would recognize for sure…

Question: What evidence is there for an ancient pre-flood civilization 11500 years ago?
Answer: We have to discuss a lot on this question. And to take the bull by the horns, let’s start with the flood. I assume you refer to Noah’s flood as described in the Bible and the Mesopotamian stories. The scientific evidence (better said, the lack of it) tells a different story; there is no evidence of a universal flood. However, there are suggestions of local geophysical events that may (hypothetically) support the story. The most popular among them is the Black Sea Deluge. In this hypothesis, based on the lack of pre-historic settlements in North Turkey, a catastrophic inflow of Mediterranean seawater into the Black Sea freshwater occurred around 6800 BCE. Unfortunately (for its believers) this hypothesis has been debunked 🤷‍♀️. Another, less popular but more plausible is the Altai flood at the end of the Ice Age (~12,000–9,000 years ago), which also, matches the date in your question. Were there civilizations back then? I copy from Civilization: Civilization (from the Latin civis=citizen and civitas=city) is a term applied to any society that has developed a writing system, government, production of surplus food, division of labor, and urbanization. The term is difficult to define because not all 'civilizations' include every one of the above facets. The term is often used, therefore, to suggest a highly developed culture. So, we are looking for communities in organized permanently inhabited urban centers that produce their food (meaning they cultivate land). So far, we have no evidence of such settlements. The people who built Gobleki Tepe and similar sites (11,500–8,000 BCE) and the Natufians before them (15,000–11,500 BCE) were still semi-sedentary populations. No matter how impressive are the findings of the Epipaleolithic and the Early Neolithic, we can’t name their civilizations. The Sumerians (~4,000 BCE) still hold the title of the first civilization ever. footnotes

Question: Coded message from an alien civilization being the ultimate in movie fantasy, what is the most interesting text you have found which needed translation and was translating to it's actual meaning really worth the effort?
Answer: "6EQUJ5" is the most famous (believed to be a coded) message we know of and came from outer space. It is mostly known as the Wow! signal. Back in the late 70s, when the search for extraterrestrial intelligent life was at its peak, Ohio State University’s Big Ear radio telescope recorded a one-of-the-kind narrowband radio signal. It —seems—to come from the constellation of Sagittarius and lasted for the full 72-second window during which Big Ear was able to observe it, and nothing similar has ever been recorded since. Astronomer Jerry R. Ehman discovered the anomaly a few days later while reviewing the recorded data. He was so impressed by the result that he circled on the computer printout the reading of the signal's intensity, "6EQUJ5", and wrote the comment "Wow!" beside it, leading to the event's widely used name. The Wow! signal represented as "6EQUJ5" is preserved by Ohio History Connection. The signal was received 47 years ago (1977) and although still undeciphered, the odds are it was an Earth-sourced one. However, the popularity it gained right away, revealed the longing of ordinary people (apart from the scientists) to communicate with extraterrestrial civilizations. Given that the extraterrestrial origin of the signal has not been completely ruled out, perhaps someday the signal will prove to be the most significant thing we've ever come across. Question: What was the reason for the presence of many foreigners in Ancient Greece and Rome?
Answer: People in antiquity migrated for the same reasons as today, better work opportunities or seeking political asylum. Now, the rest of the question is totally wrong! During the archaic and classical periods, the ancient Greek city-states (ancient Greece was not one state) didn’t attract many foreigners. In addition, there were a lot of Greek cities outside of the Greek peninsula. Some exceptions were the rich ones among them such as Athens (most of the time), Corinth, or Syracuse, where mainly artisans and philosophers could find a larger audience or clientele. However, at the same time, Egypt attracted way more foreigners, only the Greek trade station of Heracleion and the colony of Naucratis counted more than 15,000 people, and if we count the Phoenician traders and the mercenaries in Egypt, the number of foreigners goes very high. Since the Hellenistic period, when travel became easier and the strict rules about foreigners loosened in most cities, people sought a better life abroad more frequently. Then again, the Hellenistic cities such as Alexandria, Pergamon, and Antioch were the most popular destinations. Rome did attract foreigners for the reasons mentioned above.

Question: Did Greeks form/are the sea peoples, team up to siege Troy. Did the Greeks/Anatolian's cause the collapse by invading or was it metal, etc? Was everyone raiding at the time? did sea peoples invade Greece, caused the collapse of Mycenaea or Dorian?

Judge for yourselves: The Sea Peoples include Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, Tjeker and Sherden. Well?? Question: Why did the Earth form at the time period it did?
Answer: Scientists have estimated when Earth was formed although they don’t know the exact way. However, there is a dominant theory, the core accretion model. In brief, the process that formed planets, moons, asteroids, and comets: The late-stage phase of planet formation with protoplanets and planetismals is seen in this artist's depiction. (Image credit: Ashley Norris/Oxford University) Our solar system was just a cloud of dust and gas known as a solar nebula until, ~4.6 billion years ago, its material began to spin fast enough, so that its matter condensed and formed the sun in the center of the nebula. The remaining material started to clump up by gravity. The solar wind, a constant stream of charged particles that emanate from the sun's upper atmosphere, swept away lighter elements, such as hydrogen and helium, leaving behind heavy materials that formed rocky planets like Earth. One finding that has helped to strengthen core accretion's legitimacy as an explanation for planet formation is the 2005 discovery of a giant planet with a massive core orbiting the sun-like star HD 149026. As Dr. Greg Henry, the astronomer at Tennessee State University, Nashville, who detected the dimming of the star stated: "This is a confirmation of the core accretion theory for planet formation and evidence that planets of this kind should exist in abundance" The swept-away light elements formed the gas giant planets further away, where the solar wind had less impact. However, although the core accretion theory explains well the formation of the rocky planets, the gas giants are the weak part of it. The major problem is that developing gas giants through core accretion takes too long. According to the best current models, the process requires several million years longer than the typical observed lifetime of the stellar gas disks from which planets are born. So, another theory was suggested, the disk instability model: A visualization of a dusty disk orbiting a young star. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Clumps of dust and gas bind together early in the solar system's existence. Over time, these clumps can slowly compact into a giant planet. These planets can form faster than those that form within the core accretion explanation, sometimes in as little as a thousand years, which allows them to trap the rapidly-vanishing lighter gases. These planets also quickly reach an orbit-stabilizing mass that keeps them from death-marching into the sun. The exoplanetary astronomer Paul Wilson explains: If disk instability dominates the formation of planets, it should produce a wide number of worlds at large orders. The four giant planets orbiting at significant distances around the star HD 9799 provide observational evidence for disk instability. Scientists continue to study planets inside and outside of the solar system, hoping that they will understand better the formation of the planets…we are looking forward to it. further reading

Question: Is Ikaria, Greece worth seeing?
Answer: Ikaria is a unique island, nothing like the dry but cosmopolitan Cyclades, the usual image of a Greek island. Its name is associated with the myth of Icarus, that eternal symbol of youthful enthusiasm and the pursuit of freedom. These characteristics seem to have been adopted by the hospitable Ikarians, who are distinguished by their optimistic and carefree approach to life. Known as the island of longevity, Ikaria is one of the top five regions in the world for life expectancy, a phenomenon that has long been the subject of scientific study. The island is famous for its natural beauty, a mosaic of dense vegetation, streams, thermal springs (some are radioactive), idyllic fishing villages, and picturesque mountain settlements with authentic traditions. The beaches of Ikaria take the breath away with their exotic landscapes, while its mountains offer unique trails for hiking and exploring. Ikaria also has a winemaking tradition that dates back to Homeric times, the local Pramnian wine is produced with the same method and continues to produce fine wines to this day. Ikaria is a favorite destination for alternative tourism. It promises quiet vacations with countless outdoor activities, but also Dionysian experiences at the famous village festivals (panegyria) that go on until morning. So, what can you do in Ikaria? You can swim, of course. You can discover the hidden beauties of the island’s interior through its trails. The forest in the central Ikaria is the oldest in the Balkans. Its greatest treasure is a rare five-million-year-old species of oak tree called the Aria, which is native to Ikaria. Halaris Gorge is also a must. Get a treatment in the natural thermal waters of the island, which have been famous since antiquity. There are hot springs in eight different locations on Ikaria, the most well-known being in Therma, the island’s main spa town. An ancient spa. A spring in the sea Something more conservative… The food is also special, forget about souvlaki and moussaka. You’ll taste soufiko, a medley of roasted vegetables, while the traditional Ikarian pies are justly famous. Be sure to try hortopita (with wild greens), tabouropita (with pumpkin), and fouskopita (with green pepper and melted cheese). Other homegrown favourites include kathoura (goat’s cheese), roasted or boiled raska (wild goat), the stuffed goat with rice, and the unique kolokasi, a gourmet root vegetable that grows on the island and is usually served with onion and a simple vinaigrette dressing accompanied by a garlic dip. Finally, as Ikaria is not an island depending on tourism, to know it better you have to meet the Ikarians. And the best way for it is to attend a festivity…(wrong expression, you have to participate too). The video below is from an Ikarian festivity and the participants dance Ikariotiko, a local dance. This is Ikaria in brief, a magical place. It’s up to you to decide if you like magic 🤷‍♀️. Disclaimer: I don’t own any of the images nor the video.

Question: Why was Aesop a social and political genius?
Answer: Aesop has been a legend since he appeared in the world of literature. His life is as mythical as his stories, we don’t know for real who he was (if he ever existed). Plaster cast of a Hellenistic statue thought to depict Aesop; original in the Art Collection of the Villa Albani, Rome. Image credit: User:Shakko - Wikimedia Commons Aesop's biographical information lies between myth and history. Information about his life is given by many ancient and later writers (Herodotus, Aristophanes, Plato, Aristotle, Xenophon, Diodorus Siculus, Dion Chrysostom, Plutarch, Hermogenes, Lucian, Aelianos, Maximus Planudes, Nikiforos Grigoras, Andronikos Nucius, George Aitolos, etc.). According to them, Aesop was born in Phrygia (or Thrace or Sardis or Egypt) in the 6th c. BCE, meaning he wasn’t a Greek but came to Greece as a slave, bought by the Samian philosopher Xanthos. His master, impressed by his intellectual abilities, set him free. So, Aesop, the ugly, disabled outcast, met with kings and sagas such as King Croesus and Solon the Athenian. His fables are usually short narratives, containing speech or dialogue, in which animals mainly but also gods, humans, or plants are the heroes. The short narration is followed by an "epimyth", which encapsulates the allegorical meaning of the myth, with a didactic objective. However, Aesop was not the first one to use animals in his narration (a lot of older Greek myths did it), what makes his stories special? Aesop’s fables are written in prose at a time when epics and poetry were thriving. His pleasant metaphors permit the socially weak to actually protest indirectly against the socially powerful. In other words, he was the first to realize the fundamental rule of satire “A satirical writer is someone who will tell a harsh truth in front of their audience and make it out of the room alive.” And this makes him definitely a genius. The Castaway Man, an Aesop’s fable A rich Athenian was traveling by boat with others. Suddenly there was a storm and the ship sank. While everyone else was swimming, he kept calling on Athena, promising her a lot of offerings, if she helped him escape. Then one of his fellow castaways who was swimming beside him, said to him; "With Athena and (move) your hands!" Epimythion: Those who fall into calamities must themselves labor on their behalf and then beg the gods to help them.

Question: Were there any Greek/European civilisations that were even older than Minoa and Cyclades?
Answer: Hmm, maybe yes. In the early 3rd millennium BCE, not only the Minoans in Crete and the islanders in the Cyclades started to shape into civilizations but two more regions of the Aegean also developed. In mainland Greece, the Helladic civilization started to form (later evolved into the Mycenaean civilization) and a fourth distinctive one appeared on the islands of the North Aegean (Lemnos, Lesvos, Chios, Skyros, etc). Although the four Aegean civilizations started almost simultaneously, the Northern islanders started earlier, reaching their peak ~2,800 BCE. They had larger arable lands than the Cyclades, closer to the coast of Asia Minor from where they secured resources, independence in the agricultural economy due to the morphology of the terrain and geographical location, made sea communication between the northern and southern Aegean safe. The islands had become supply stations for the ships of the era. The most important settlements were Poliochni of Lemnos, Thermi of Lesbos, Emporio of Chios, Heraion of Samos, and Palamari of Skyros. Unfortunately, earthquakes and the rise of the Minoans put an end to this little-known but fascinating civilization around 2,000 BCE. The archaeological site of Poliochni. Question: What was it like to be a Greek living under Roman rule?
Answer: The Greek lifestyle didn’t change much superficially. The clever Romans left seemingly untouched most of the Greek institutions (citizen’s assembly, Voule, etc) giving them the illusion they were still decided for their affairs. That wasn’t true, their decisions had to be under Roman law and they had to worship the Emperor, a new kind of relationship between a citizen and the ruler for most of them. By the time of Constantine the Great, the democratic institutions had become a caricature although the Assembly was never abandoned. Bronze statue of the Roman Emperor Augustus (27 BC – 14 AD); found in the Aegean Sea Creative Commons - Wikipedia They had to co-exist with Roman immigrants (or colonizers in some cases). Gradually, a lot of Roman habits passed in Greece, like the Roman spectacles of the arena—almost all the Greek theaters were altered so that they could host such games (only the theaters in Epidaurus and Larissa kept the original architecture). The theater, already of lower quality than the classical period, declined even more becoming a cheap spectacle. The Roman architecture succeeded the Hellenistic one in public and private constructions. Roman ruins in Athens gus619USA's User Profile | Atlas Obscura A lot of specialized Greeks (doctors, artists, architects, etc) migrated to Italy as the demand for Greek artifacts and services increased there. However, very few Greeks ever reached high-ranked offices of the Roman regime. Sarcophagus with a Greek Physician | Roman | The Metropolitan Museum of Art It was a mutual trade of culture that ended in many Greek customs adapted by the Romans (the Roman colonizers were totally Hellenized) and the Romanizing of the Greeks. Were the Greeks happy under the Roman rule? Yes, in a way. The Pax Romana and the wealth that followed it made them finally accept the Romans although they always felt the bitterness that their rulers were less civilized than themselves. This bitterness grew when Christianity prevailed in the empire. Greek was thought as a synonym for pagan and scorned for this.

Question: How many ancient temples were destroyed during the Byzantine Empire?
Answer: I think I have to rephrase the question. What the OP means is “How many pagan temples were destroyed by the Christians during the Roman Empire?” (the term “Byzantine Empire” doesn’t correspond to a real state, as Emilios Panoussopoulos noted). Well, if you think that the Christians destroyed all temples, you are wrong. If you think that the Christians didn’t influence the fate of the ancient temples, you are wrong again. Actually, a lot of different things happened. There were the “lucky” temples They were the monumental temples in urban regions (like the Pantheon and the Parthenon) that were converted into Christian churches. Of course, the pagan sculptures were removed or damaged. The 12th metope of the East side of the Parthenon depicts Aphrodite. Copyright The Hellenic Ministry of Culture Before the conversion of the Parthenon to a church, the figures on the metopes were hacked by a thick chisel so that only the outlines remained. The metopes on the south side escaped this religious barbarism, together with the last one on the north side. This last one particularly got it away because of its theme, one woman seated and another standing. It was interpreted as the Annunciation to the Virgin, giving it a new, Christian dimension, and thus it escaped destruction. Apart from “accidents” like the above, these temples/churches survived almost intact to our days as they remained functional and were repaired when needed.
