Question: Could the foundation of the city of Rome be possibly older than the generally accepted year of 753 B.C.?
Answer: Only on specific occasions, such as colonization, cities are founded on virgin ground and Rome is not a colony. As a settlement, predates the given date by far. Yes, there is an explanation for this. Cities (or mere settlements) are not designed, they evolve. People find a good land spot to inhabit, settle there, expand it, organize it, make it thrive and/or decline. The same happened to Rome. There is archaeological evidence of human occupation of the Rome area from at least 5,000 years, but the dense layer of much younger debris obscures Palaeolithic and Neolithic sites. In the Sant’ Omobono area of Rome (to jump to a more recent period) lies a series of religious buildings that defined the site for much of the first millennium BCE. The Archaic temple found there is dated ~8–5 century BCE, that is, it is built earlier than the accepted date of 753 BCE. (Courtesy Dan Diffendale/Sant'Omobono Project) Oldest known temple remains in Rome (7th-6th century BCE) There is also an explanation on why the Romans didn’t claim an earlier foundation of their city. They simply followed a common rule of antiquity; the foundation of a city was attributed to a divine entity or to hero of divine origin and in this way, they raised their status. What is more, it is no coincidence that in 753 BCE started the period of the seven kings of Rome (with Romulus being the first, according to the legend). It is the period that the city became a significant one and its history is recorded. A little later, no legends were needed, Rome became a legend herself. footnotes

Question: Why is Dionysus so important?
Answer: He isn’t, how many times have you thought of him in the last month? But there was a time that he was, back in antiquity. Even then, this peculiar deity changed his persona all the time. Ready for a trip in the past? Bacchus by Caravaggio. Oil on canvas by Caravaggio, 1596–97; in the Uffizi Gallery, Florence Dionysos is the god of multiple aspects and contradictions. His nature is bipolar and he often exhibits diametrically opposite aspects. Before delving into his soul, let’s introduce him. He is the son of Zeus and Semele, the only woman Zeus ever loved. Hera was determined to find and kill the boy, so even as a child Dionysos had to hide and travel all over the world—he reached India and even died once—learned a lot, got into adventures, and finally, returned to Greece as the god of wine, vegetation, pleasure, festivity, madness and wild frenzy. He was depicted as either an older, bearded god or an effeminate, long-haired youth or even as a child (the interpretation of Caravaggio is brilliant and the closest to the ancient spirit, as his Bacchus is a boy with muscular, man’s arms). The truth is that that bright, cheerful god, was an entity of the Underworld when he first appeared back in the Mycenaeans’ times. Later, he became milder and gifted the Greeks with wine, giving them a way out of grief and sadness. These two opposite qualities are combined in theater. He is the god associated with the wildness of nature, vegetation, and the world of beasts, while at the same time expressing civilization and the subjugation of nature to man through the making of wine. A return to the "animal passion" of nature takes place, away from the limitations imposed by rationalization. He reveals himself to his followers through the onset of mania, and in this way, they partake in his divine essence, while he can also redeem those possessed by it. He is also very associated with fulfilled love, and Anacreon's epigram to the god begins with the words "O Lord, whose companions in the game are mighty Eros, the black-eyed nymphs, and Aphrodite!” He is the god who drives away every worry and sorrow from humans, while at the same time being wild, terrifying, and of horrific nature. He is the destroyer of the household and simultaneously the one who unites the community. Finally, as a divine entity, he transcends man and his mortal nature, yet at the same time resembles him, as he experiences death. Dionysos, when appears in his worship with the phallus, the tree, or the bull as his emblem, is the god of fertility and protector of crops, especially the vine. He may also be the enthusiastic Dionysos, with emblems of the thyrsus and the torch, as well as the retinue of the Maenads, the Bacchae, the Thyiades, and the Bassarides, as conveyed by the mythological narrative. So, why Dionysos was important? Because he impersonated all of the many human personas…

Question: How did some ancient cities disappear? E.g troy, it was a big city but then after the war it fell from history and got covered by dirt for us to dig it up. Why didn't anyone else use that location to build again? (expanded question below)
Answer: Believe it or not, only nature can make a city disappear. Avalanches (like what happened to Aiges), submersions (like Pavlopetri), lava flow (Pompeii) are the reasons for a city to vanish. Destruction by human activity — war, or riots— or even earthquakes can result in temporary abandonment, and then life returns and the damaged cities are rebuilt. Pavlopetri was a Mycenaean city and port that submerged for natural causes ~1,000 BCE. Underwater city Pavlopetri – Laconia. Why? A settlement is created for a reason, it’s a port or the residence of the ruler or it’s simply close to a water source, and people don’t abandon them easily. Look what happened to Corinth, for instance; the Romans razed the city in 146 BCE but rebuilt it a hundred years later as it is a strategic spot. The same happened to Troy; the first settlement was founded ~3,600 BCE and turned into a city ~3,000 BCE. Nine times the city was destroyed by invasions and earthquakes and rebuilt afterward until it was finally abandoned in 500 CE after a strong earthquake. The earthquake was not the real reason for the abandonment. Troy lived for millennia because of its strategic location, it controlled the trade routes between the Aegean and the Black Sea. At the time of the final disaster, other ports (mainly Constantinople) had replaced its significance. The probable location of the ancient city of Troy. Provided by Graham Bartholomew/BBC/Wild Mercury Productions Even when a city is eventually abandoned (because some other location has replaced its importance or its resources have run out) it takes centuries if not millennia to be buried. Take Mycenae for instance, the Bronze Age citadel was never buried. A gravure by E. Breton (1846), decades before Schliemann’s excavation. Porte Des Lions a Mycenes

Question: How did the ancient Greek concept of democracy differ from modern democratic systems?
Answer: It is like comparing apples and oranges. The obvious difference is that the ancient states had direct democracy (the citizens not only had the right to elect and be elected to offices but also legislated and judged) whereas the modern regimes are republics, that is, the citizens participate in governance through representatives. (Of course, anything else is impossible in our time, given the large-scale and populous states). However, the true difference is deeper. To start with, look at the official names of the ancient states. The name of the Athenian state is not Athens, but rather the Athenians or the people of Athens (i.e., the demos of Athens); the name of the Macedonian state, a kingdom, is the Macedonians; the name of Sparta is not Sparta or Lacedaemon but the Lacedaemonians (not Spartans!). How the ancient Greek states named themselves, that is, how they defined their identity, reveals a fundamental characteristic of them (both democratic regimes and kingdoms): they identified themselves with their citizens (not with their inhabitants in general). In short, an ancient state is the sum of its citizens and its rulers, as well as the lands that are the property of the citizens (whether private or public). Decree of Athenian Assembly Let's make a comparison with the naming of modern states. The name of a state can consist of a simple geographical designation (the name of Japan is Nippon), a designation of the political system accompanied by a geographical name (the name of Great Britain is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland), and of course, the name of America is the United States of America (not of Americans). This shows that in the mindset of the citizens of modern states, there is a deeply rooted perception that, at best, the state is something that exists above and apart from the citizen, it is an abstract entity. This perception is related to the history of the state and its institutions in modern times. When a modern person—let’s say a modern Greek— refers to the Greek state, they do not consider themselves as part of this state—unlike when they refer to Greece as their native country or their compatriots. An ancient Greek could not make this distinction because when an Athenian refers to their state, that is, to the Athenians or the people of Athens, they automatically consider themselves a part of the Athenians and the people of Athens. To understand better the distinction between the state and the citizen, I’ll give you an example from the Greek Constitution. The State is entitled to demand from all citizens the fulfillment of the duty of social and national solidarity. (Article 25.4). To see the difference between this modern perception of the state and the ancient perception, an Athenian text could not even articulate these ideas, and if it did, it would phrase them as follows: "The rulers of the Athenians are executors of the will of the Athenians (or the people of Athens)," meaning not that the rulers of the state are executors of the will of the state and serve the Athenians, but rather that "the people of Athens or the Athenians are entitled to demand from all Athenians the fulfillment of the duty of social and national solidarity." To conclude, we often forget how young the modern democratic regimes are. The majority of Europe's population for much of the 20th century did not live in parliamentary democracies but in dictatorships, one-party regimes, and monarchies. On the contrary, in the case of ancient Greece, we can look back on an experience of either moderate or extreme democracies that spans a period of 700 or more years, from the late 6th century BCE, mainly in Athens, to around the beginning of the 3rd century CE. Even within the framework of the Roman Empire, there were communities of citizens who still maintained democratic institutions, regardless of whether power was monopolized by members of a wealthy elite. In an era where the challenges to democratic institutions are particularly heightened due to populism and demagogy, the crisis of political parties, the uncontrolled spread of fake news on the internet, and the misconception that social media is somehow a kind of virtual universal replica of the ancient people's assembly (ekklesia), it is useful to turn to ancient democracies not as the pilgrimage of a monument but as a study of an experience that gives us food for thought. I rest my case.

Question: Can you tell me about The Dance of Apollo and Dionysus?
Answer: It is a clever metaphor by Nietzsche in his work The Birth of Tragedy to prove that the Greek tragedy was the only point in history when two opposing tensions, the “Apollonian” and the “Dionysian” were brought together. In Greek mythology, Apollo was the god of light, protector of music, poetry, and prophecy. Honored in temples and oracles like the Delphi, he is sober, elegant, and eloquent. In Nietzsche’s book, he represents the reason. On the other hand, Dionysus was associated with death and rebirth, fertility, wine-making, ritual madness. To accompany Dionysus was not an easy thing; the followers of Dionysus were both women and men, who are often depicted as mad and or intoxicated. He is the “irrational”. The dance of the Bacchants, by Charles Gleyre, 1849, via Musée cantonal des Beaux-Arts, Lausanne The Birth of Tragedy is an essay on aesthetics. One of the book’s main premises is that “only as an aesthetic phenomenon is an existence and the world eternally justified”. Nietzschean philosophy traditionally sees existence as pain and chaos. Only art can make this pain bearable and Nietzsche finds that there are two artistic paths within art, the Apollonian and the Dionysian. After exploring them thoroughly, he concludes that the Greek tragedy was the only point in history when these two opposing tensions were brought together. For Nietzsche, Apollo is a deity related to calmness and reason. Dionysus is the god who embodies the experience of the drunken reality. Based on illusions or misrepresentations, drunken reality is instinctive. Unlike the structured, ordered illusion of the dream, drunkenness is deeply emotional and irrational. Within this chaotic reality, the subject is dissolved, becoming one with its surroundings. As a result, drunkenness is an experience of oneness or as Nietzsche calls it primordial unity. Theatre evolved out of the dithyramb, a ritual hymn including dancing, in honor of Dionysus. Thespis was the first person in history to step out of the dithyramb’s singularity. He began speaking in verse as an individual and representing a certain character. This was the birth of tragedy. Due to this special origin story, the ancient Greek tragedy was always a combination of epic and lyric poetry. Photo from Euripides' Bacchae directed by Alexis Minotis. Βάκχες του Ευριπίδη, μια από τις πιο αινιγματικές τραγωδίες της αρχαιοελληνικής γραμματείας | LiFO In the dithyramb, Nietzsche’s philosophy saw a purely Dionysian endeavor. Thespis’ stepping out of the dithyramb to embody a certain character was a process of individuation and, as a result, an Apollonian intrusion. Consequently, the Greek tragedy was born out of the fusion or rather the dialectic synthesis of the Apollonian and the Dionysian. Question: How does dark matter influence the universe?
Answer: Although we don’t know what dark matter is, we know what it does. Galaxies in our universe seem to be achieving an impossible feat. They are rotating with such speed that the gravity generated by their observable matter could not possibly hold them together; they should have torn themselves apart long ago. The same is true of galaxies in clusters, which leads scientists to believe that something we cannot see is at work. They think something we have yet to detect directly is giving these galaxies extra mass, generating the extra gravity they need to stay intact. This strange and unknown matter was called “dark matter” since it is not visible. Ordinary matter such as that in planets, stars, and galaxies, comprises only some 5 percent of the universe. Dark matter accounts for roughly a quarter, while dark energy is the largest component of the cosmos. Credit: Astronomy: Roen Kelly, after NIST Are the percentages of dark matter and dark energy stable? Some facts about dark matter: Unlike normal matter, dark matter does not interact with the electromagnetic force. This means it does not absorb, reflect, or emit light, making it extremely hard to spot. Researchers have been able to infer the existence of dark matter only from the gravitational effect it seems to have on visible matter. Dark matter seems to outweigh visible matter roughly six to one, making up about 27% of the universe. The matter we know and that makes up all stars and galaxies only accounts for 5% of the content of the universe! What dark matter may be: A theory is that it could contain "supersymmetric particles" – hypothesized particles that are partners to those already known in the Standard Model. Other theories suggest physics beyond the Standard Model, such as supersymmetry and extra dimensions. One theory suggests the existence of a “Hidden Valley”, a parallel world made of dark matter having very little in common with the matter we know. Can we detect it? Many theories say the dark matter particles would be light enough to be produced at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in Cern. If they were created at the LHC, they would escape through the detectors unnoticed. However, they would carry away energy and momentum, so physicists could infer their existence from the amount of energy and momentum “missing” after a collision.

Question: What role did the ancient Minoans’ primitive form of currency play in the centrally controlled palatial economy?
Answer: The Minoan economy was pre-monetary and based on bartering without any use of money. Minoan Bronze balance pans and lead weighs of various sizes from Akrotiri, Thera. They are displayed in the Archaeological Museum of Athens. How did they trade? By weighing the commodities. Knowing the weight of a commodity provides a way to value goods in the marketplace. There are found weighs made of hematite, and a lot of them were imported. This indicates that they were standard weights, and there were obviously local stone equivalents that matched their weight. In addition, the local merchants had to be familiar with the metric systems of other cities. The trade between the central administration and the local traders must be done similarly. Numerous seals found indicate they were used to mark goods and Linear B tablets provide us with lists of goods that individuals or towns offered as taxation. The person then, could take commodities of equivalent value. The Linear B tablet from Knossos (KN L 693) is about the distribution of tunics. However, there is another theory; according to a study published January 20, 2020 in the open-access journal PLOS ONE by Maikel H. G. Kuijpers and Cătălin N. Popa of Leiden University, Netherlands. Money is an important feature of modern human society. One key feature of money is standardization, but this can be difficult to identify in the archaeological record since ancient people had inexact forms of measurement compared with today. In this study, the authors assessed possible money from the Early Bronze Age of Central Europe, comparing the objects based on their perceived -- if not precise -- similarity. The objects studied were made of bronze in shapes described as rings, ribs, and axe blades. The authors examined more than 5,000 such objects from more than 100 ancient hoards. They statistically compared the objects' weights using a psychological principle known as the Weber fraction, which quantifies the concept that, if objects are similar enough in mass, a human being weighing them by hand can't tell the difference. They found that even though the objects' weights varied, around 70% of the rings were similar enough to have been indistinguishable by hand (averaging about 195 grams), as were subsets of the ribs and axe blades. The authors suggest that this consistent similarity in shape and weight, along with the fact that these objects often occurred in hoards, are signs of their use as an early form of standardized currency. Later, in the Middle Bronze Age of Europe, more precise weighing tools appear in the archaeological record along with an increase in scrap bronze, pointing to a developed system of weighing. The authors add: "The euros of Prehistory came in the form of bronze rings, ribs and axes. These Early Bronze Age artifacts were standardized in shape and weight and used as an early form of money." My personal opinion is that this theory needs more evidence. Most of those items are found in tombs and I don’t know anyone that would bury a check.

Question: What is the effect of being near a black hole, but not inside it? Does time slow down for objects near a black hole?
Answer: If the object manages to escape, yes, time will slow down for it. But let’s take it from the start, here is our black hole: our black hole’s event horizon spans about millions of miles A flat, swirling cloud of hot, glowing gas called an accretion disk surrounds it and so do glowing structures called photon rings, which form closer to the black hole from light that has orbited it one or more times. As the object approaches the black hole, reaching speeds ever closer to that of light, the glow from the accretion disk and background stars becomes amplified in much the same way as the sound of an oncoming racecar rises in pitch. Their light appears brighter and whiter when looking into the direction of travel. Along the way, the black hole’s disk, photon rings, and the night sky become increasingly distorted — and even form multiple images as their light traverses the increasingly warped space-time. As the object approaches closer and orbits around the hole, space-time becomes ever more distorted closer to the horizon, it will slow down and then seem to freeze (This is why astronomers originally referred to black holes as “frozen stars.”). If the object crosses the horizon, its destruction by spaghettification is just seconds away. If it doesn’t and escapes to safety, we, the observers, will measure a different time compared to that of the object. That’s because time passes more slowly near a strong gravitational source and when moving near the speed of light. Take a tour of an alternative visualization that tracks a camera as it approaches, falls toward, briefly orbits, and escapes a supermassive black hole. This immersive 360-degree version allows viewers to look around during the flight. Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center/J. Schnittman and B. Powell

Question: Which was the "international" role of the cycladic islands in the Neolithic period? Were there exportations of its stones, in raw form, or in some crafted form?
Answer: The Cycladic islands, although uninhabited until ~5,500 BCE had a material necessary for tool construction, obsidian. And as "There is no early farming village in the Near East that doesn't get obsidian"(C. Renferew) the “international” role of these islands is certain. Obsidian is a natural black glass which originates exclusively from geologically young volcanic regions. The obsidian sources in the eastern Mediterranean are rare and have been traced on certain islands of the Cyclades, on Melos(the main source of obsidian) and Antiparos. ( Nisyros and Yiali in the East Aegean were also sources of obsidian that was distributed mainly to Asia Minor and the islands of the North Aegean). The Melian obsidian was already being used by the end of the Upper Palaeolithic (9th millennium BCE) to produce blades with sharp edges to serve as knives, scrapers and razors in an extended area: Distribution of obsidian from the island of Melos in the Neolithic. Image from https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Distribution-of-obsidian-from-the-island-of-Melos-in-the-Neolithic_fig10_273356054 Melian obsidian found in habitation levels of the Upper Palaeolithic at Franchthi Cave in Hermionid has provided evidence that navigation in the Aegean had already begun by the 9th millennium BCE. The extraction and the transportation of obsidian at the end of the Palaeolithic and during most of the Neolithic Period (ca. 6800-3200 BCE) was not carried out by populations permanently settled close to the quarries of Melos, but by more specialized groups who reached the island from settlements of central and south Aegean. According to a prevailing view based on the study of obsidian artefacts (cores, flakes and tools) from archaeological sites of central and southern Greece, after extraction a preliminary and on-the-spot retouch of the raw material followed at least during the Early and Middle Neolithic (ca. 6800-5300 BC). During the Late and the Final Neolithic (ca. 5300-3200 BC), when the systematic habitation of the Cyclades developed, the transportation of obsidian changed and was incorporated into the gradually developing trade networks of the Aegean. Obsidian reached then other settlements, outside the Cyclades, in the form of roughly retouched cores. footnotes Obsidian Early_Neolithic_settlement_patterns_and_exchange_n.pdf Milos - Wikipedia

Question: How did ancient Egyptians add the final touches to their makeup?
Answer: Makeup was very important in ancient Egypt, both men and women used it not only for aesthetics but for hygiene reasons as well. The characteristic black eyeliner, for instance (kohl) protected the eyes from the desert sun's glare. In addition, it contained malachite (a copper carbonate pigment) and galena (a natural mineral form of lead), both beneficial for protection from infection and bugs. The Egyptian beauty kit also contained a paste based on red ochre clay used as a lipstick and blusher plus creams and balms for skin treatment, perfumes, henna to make up the nails, hands, and feet, and more. All these were applied on the face with brushes (lipstick), sticks (eyeliner), or even pads for powder. Merit's cosmetic box; circa 1390-1352 BCE. The little cylinder with the stick in it was her eyeliner. It is displayed in Museo Egizio (Turin) Image credit: Attribution 2.0 Italy However, as every woman knows, it is impossible to draw the characteristic Egyptian line without looking at your face. Italian conservator Lorenza D'Alessandro restoring a mural of the Egyptian Queen Nefertari. Image via Archaeology & Art (@archaeologyart) on X The solution was simple; either a servant or member of the family applied it for them or used a mirror. Painting from the tomb of Nakht depicts three women helping each other to makeup (Google images) Bronze vanity mirror, 18th Dynasty, approx. 1539-1292 B.C. Private collection Later on, there even were compact mirrors image credit © National Museums Scotland Mirror Of course, all the above cosmetics, manufactured professionally and sold in the marketplace, were expensive items that only the upper class could afford. Question: What if our understanding of physics is fundamentally flawed, and there's an entirely new set of laws waiting to be discovered?
Answer: Physics examines natural phenomena and attempts, through laws, to measure and predict them. Mistakes can occur in the observation of phenomena (for example, the once very popular Rutherford's atomic model has been surpassed for decades) as better instruments and better experiments can potentially overturn an existing perception. So, yes, our understanding of what’s going on around us can be flawed. It’s quite an improvement, right? However, the laws themselves are immutable; they can only be expanded to include new phenomena (for instance, quantum mechanics studies phenomena of the microcosm that have no correspondence in our dimensions, but the tools we use remain the same: conservation of momentum, energy, etc.). The reason is simple; we use mathematics to describe the laws. Note: There they made a big mistake in the early stages of physics (meaning in classical antiquity); they did not make a mathematical representation of their ideas, resulting in erroneous laws. Of course, this hasn't been happening for centuries, so you can rest assured that the physics you study is correct.

Question: How did Bronze Age people get iron metal?
Answer: Iron was not a popular metal during the Bronze Age for a good reason; although iron oxides were in abundance, the high temperatures needed for the production of the metal were out of their reach, they simply couldn’t produce iron. They didn’t bother anyway, as copper alloys did the job pretty well. However, some iron objects dated to the Bronze Age do exist. These extremely rare items are made with meteoric iron processed by forging. Albert Jambon, as part of his work at the Institut de minéralogie, de physique des matériaux et de cosmochimie (CNRS / UPMC / IRD / Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle), has demonstrated that iron used during the Bronze Age is always meteoric conducting nondestructive chemical analyses of samples using a portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometer. Beads from meteoric iron, from Gerzeh, Egypt. They are dated c. 3,200 BCE and are the oldest iron objects found so far. Image from https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0305440313002057 The iron dagger of Tutankhamun. Image from A new origin story for King Tut’s meteorite dagger The Iron Age began ~1200 BCE when the lack of tin (necessary for copper alloys) forced people in Anatolia and Caucasus to invest in improving the smelting methods. As terrestrial iron ores were far more abundant and easier to procure, the use of meteoric metal was abandoned. footnotes https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0305440317301322 Bronze Age artifacts used meteoric iron

Question: How did Phillip II of Macedon change ancient Greek history?
Answer: Philip II wasn’t supposed to be a king as he was the youngest of the three sons of King Amyntas III. Fate, however, had different plans for him. His older brothers perished (Alexander II was assassinated and Perdiccas III was killed fighting the Illyrians), and in 359 BCE, Philip, with the unanimous consent of the Macedonian army as always, ascended the throne. This prince, who was initially meant to be only a general proved to have an ambitious vision for significant changes in the political landscape of the Greek world. And what was the political landscape at the moment? The leading city-states had become puppets of the Persian Empire. Persia, exploiting their desperate need for money during the Peloponnesian War, had managed to impose its terms on them (it had taken control of Asia Minor and secured their alliance in case of revolt). Philip had realized how vulnerable to the Persian hazard were not only the city-states in the South but his kingdom as well. In case of a new Persian invasion, Macedonia would be the first to fall. Philip was convinced that only united in a political entity, could the Greeks face Persia politically and militarily (he was not alone in this, more Greek politicians, like the Athenian Isocrates, believed in unification). Thus, he came up with a grandiose plan to unite them (under his leadership, of course). This astute and cultured man did not rush to address the other cities; first, he dealt with his own place. Macedonia was a fairly stable economic state but lacked the high cultural flourishing of the city-states and had little influence in political affairs. This was about to change by taking one step at a time… Gold Stater struck during the reign of Philip II, c. 340-328 BCE Step one was military renovations (new weapons, better training, and strategy). With the renewed army (along with diplomatic maneuvers), he secured calmness in the northwest border and then moved eastward towards the Athenian colonies in Thrace. The purpose was not only to "bother" the Athenians but to take control of the region's gold mines (step two) - mission accomplished. Now, having the best military force and abundant gold at his disposal, he could proceed to the main plan. The cultural "revolution" in Macedonia was at least impressive; the newly built palace/administration center in Aigai is the largest building of antiquity in the Greek world. Great artists and philosophers (such as Aristotle and Euripides) were invited to teach in Macedonia, and soon new artistic trends were created (such as realistic portraiture), which we often encounter in the Hellenistic and Roman periods (but this is the subject of another post). Meanwhile, the Macedonian military and political influence was increasingly expanding in the Greek south. Drawing restoration of the Aigai palace façade. Until 338 BCE when finally (in one way or another) the Greeks were persuaded to create the coveted alliance against the Persians, Macedonia under Philip was the main player on the Greek political scene and, more importantly, would remain in this position until the end of the Greek world, shifting the center of political decisions to the North. The great city-states of the classical era passed (and remained) in a secondary role. The alliance didn't last long; soon enough, many cities wanted to rid themselves of Macedonian hegemony. However, it became apparent to everyone that the era of small independent city-states had ended, the Hellenistic era was the era of leagues. One of the major losers of Macedonian hegemony was direct democracy. Macedonian interventions in the political affairs of their allies, as well as the creation of broader decision-making centers, weakened the importance of the institution. The Greek world became more conservative, a fact that became clear a little later with the creation of the Hellenistic kingdoms. This guy who left nothing to chance did one more thing: he ensured the proper education not only of his successor but also of the entire new generation of noble Macedonians destined for military positions (this must have been a copy of the Persian way of educating nobility). If you think Aristotle taught young Alexander by walking in the gardens of the Aigai, you are mistaken. Philip had established a military academy (gymnasium) in Mieza, a huge complex where Alexander and around 100 other young Macedonians were trained in strategy, and military tactics, and learned philosophy, poetry, etc. Imagine a kind of ancient West Point. Thus, after the unexpected death of Philip, young Alexander knew exactly what he had to do to continue with his father's work, and the camaraderie that developed among the young Macedonians proved invaluable during the campaign in the East. In other words, Philip created Alexander. The so-far excavated part of the royal gymnasium in Mieza. It covers half a square mile. To close (finally!) this post, Philip’s vision shook the Greek classical world. It was about time to take a step ahead and most of the traditionally strong states hesitated to do. Unfortunately, some of them never adopted and remained on the wrong side of history. They perished. A note: I didn’t find it useful to narrate all the battles won (or lost) by Philip. Question: Are there any abandoned archaeological sites ("abandoned for a second time")?
Answer: Yes, in fact, this is the fate for most of them. A site may be abandoned, usually reburied, when everything of historical significance is removed from it. Take as an example the humble Athenian grave in which Pericles’s cup was found. The precious cup (with Pericles’s “signature” on it) is conserved and displayed in a museum and the site is buried once more. A site can also be reburied, meaning abandoned for a while, for protection reasons. Some sites, usually the ones containing frescos, are sensitive to human presence and fresh air. After being studied they are closed again. If you have ever admired a photo of the magnificent throne of Queen Euridice of Macedonia (Alexander’s grandmother), don’t search for it in a museum, a photo is the only way to see it. It is still in the queen’s closed tomb, as light and fresh air will destroy the colors. Euridice’s throne. Image from https://gr.pinterest.com/pin/550424385691238037/ Unfortunately, some fascinating sites are abandoned out of indifference. Did you know, for instance, that an elegant Mycenaean palace was unearthed in Ithaca? Had it studied thoroughly, it might have provided evidence that the Homeric Ithaca was a real place. For unknown reasons, the excavation has stopped since 2012 and the site is abandoned (congrats to our Ministry of Culture). The so-called “Palace of Odysseus” in Ithaca. Unearthed and abandoned for a second time. Question: Has Bronze Age copper from Cyprus been found outside the Mediterranean? If so, where?
Answer: Since at least the 2nd millennium BCE, Cyprus was one of the main sources of copper for the Old World. The mineral wealth of the island (remnants of the ancient copper industry have been found in more than 40 locations) formed the basis of the island’s economic prosperity from prehistoric times until late antiquity. Cyprus (Alashiya back then) had started to export copper to the East by the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE. It is however in the Late Bronze Age that the production and export of Cypriot copper really took off. Although the Minoan Crete, the Mycenaean kingdom, Egypt, and the Canaanite cities were the main destination for the metal ingots, remnants are also found in Mesopotamia and even Central Europe. Reconstruction of a Bronze Age furnace based on archaeological data of Politico, Cyprus. Photo credit: V. Kassianidou The earliest references to Cypriot copper exports are found in texts on clay tablets from Mari and Alalakh, in present-day Syria, as well as Babylon, dating back to the 19th-17th centuries BCE. During the Late Bronze Age, various types of ingots were concurrently used. However, the most widespread was the ingot in the shape of a bull's skin, which first appeared in the 16th century BCE. They were named by archaeologists because their shape resembles a stretched bull's skin, as depicted in Egyptian wall paintings of the era. Bull’s skin-shaped ingot from Mycenae. Photo credit: Numismatic Museum of Athens From the 13th century BCE onwards, ingots of this shape are found throughout the eastern and central Mediterranean and beyond. They have been found from the palace at Dur-Kuri-galzu near Baghdad to the shores of Southern France (Séte-Hérault) and from Oberwilfingen in Germany to Qantir in Egypt. Recently, many examples have also been published from Bulgaria, apart from findings in mainland Greece, Crete, and the shipwrecks of Uluburun and N. Euboea. The shift to the Iron Age did not negatively impact the economy of Cyprus, as there continued to be demand for large quantities of copper. Cyprus, which possessed the largest copper deposits in the eastern Mediterranean along with the necessary specialized labor force and technological knowledge, did not cease production and export of copper. On the contrary, it maintained its significant position in the commercial and cultural networks of the Mediterranean, which gradually reformed. Question: If Xerxes had listened to Queen Artemisia of Caria advice and not attacked the Athenian fleet, could the Persians have won the war?
Answer: Herodotus recorded Artemisia’s advice as the following: Tell the king from me, Mardonius, this is the answer he receives from her who was neither the most timid nor the weakest in the naval battles in Euboea. Despot, it is right for me to tell you my opinion as I think about what is best for you. This is my advice for you: don't fight at sea. Their men are superior to ours at sea just as men are superior to women. Why should you run the risk of naval actions? Didn't you occupy Athens, which was the target of the campaign, didn't you occupy the rest of Greece? No one is stopping you. I'll have to explain to you how he thinks the enemy is going to go. If you do not attack but keep the fleet on the coast, or if you attack the Peloponnese, despot, you will achieve your goals effortlessly. The Greeks, who will not be able to resist you any longer, will scatter and retreat, city by city. They have no supplies on this island, as I have been informed, nor do they consider it their home. If you send an army to the Peloponnese, the Peloponnesians will not rest easy or fight in a naval battle for Athens. But if you decide to fight a naval battle, I fear that your fleet will be destroyed. Listen to that too, King. Good men usually have bad slaves while bad men have good slaves. You, as the most excellent man in the world, have evil slaves. None of these Egyptians, Cypriots, Cilicians, and Pamphilians, who say they are allies, will benefit us. Ιστορίαι (Ηροδότου)/Ουρανία She proved to be right, the naval fight was a bad decision for the Persians. It would be safer (and wiser) for them to keep on fighting on land. However, the Greek forces wouldn’t be as scattered as she thought. The Athenians had sought refuge in the Peloponnese, so their forces would have stayed loyal to the ally. In addition, the mountainous, full-of-gorges Peloponnesian terrain provides plenty of death traps for an invasion army. So, the Persians would have had much better chances had they continued fighting on land but the outcome of their campaign would be still at risk. PS. Artemisia speech’s only document is in Herodotus, therefore it is not documented enough. However, Herodotus, a Carian himself, might have interviewed fellow Carians who participated in the campaign and learned from them. Of course, we’ll never know for sure.

Question: Was theater important during Byzantine times? How about the Ottoman period? Is it still important in modern Greece and Turkey?
Answer: No, it wasn’t. In the social life of the early Byzantine period, theatrical forms of late antiquity survived, mainly the imitations of ancient tragedies and the rich production of New Comedy. Serious theater gradually begins to recede and disappear from the stage. Light pantomime shows, offering various kinds of Mimic and Pantomime entertainments, gain the preference of the audience. Theater, in its most debased form, often became a place for ridiculing and mocking the mysteries of the Christian religion (e.g., the mystery of baptism, the martyrdom of the Saints, etc.). As one of the last strong ideological supports of idolatrous spirit, it was repeatedly condemned by the official Church, vehemently. These reactions and simultaneously its decadent character likely led to its gradual disappearance during the 7th to 8th centuries CE. The hostile stance of the official Church does not satisfactorily explain the completely limited position of theater in Byzantine culture, especially considering that neither the genre of liturgical drama, which was so widespread in the medieval West, ever took root in Byzantium. The theatrical expression did not surpass, during the Byzantine centuries, the boundaries set by popular pantomime, except for the festive events that took place in the imperial court, which seem to have had, in some cases, hybrid dramatic elements, or even the rich ecclesiastical liturgy. Moreover, the architecture of the Church with the sanctuary and the three doors/entrances resembles a theatrical set, and the rituals have dramatic elements, culminating in the typicon of Holy Week. In later centuries, ancient Greek theater continues to engage cultivated individuals on a theoretical level. As I know nothing about the importance of theater in the Ottoman Empire, I copy from Early Modern Dramatic Entertainments in the Ottoman Empire: Part I | MEMOs Dramatic entertainments in early modern Ottoman Turkey were built upon several traditions and cross-cultural encounters. They were an extension of those entertainments inherited from the Seljuk Turks as famously referred to by the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene (1083-1150) in her Alexiad, an account of her father’s reign, where she describes how the Seljuk Turks impersonated the Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and made him the butt of their joke. Early modern Ottoman dramatic entertainments were also an extension of the Ottoman Turks’ encounter with foreign entertainments both at the borderlands and the many ethnic cultures within their dominion. In modern Greece, the theater has regained its former glory. In Athens alone, 152 theater halls play a significant role in cultural activities and their dynamic growth was not interrupted by the current socio-economic crisis. The National Theater of Greece, Athens, was founded in 1891. Question: The magic of winter - which art works have enchanted you?
Answer: There are many great paintings of winter scenes but nothing can match Nature herself…which is captured only in photos: Frost flowers in the Arctic Ocean Courtesy of Matthias Wietz They aren't flowers, of course. They are more like ice sculptures that grow on the border between the sea and air. The air is extremely cold and extremely dry, colder than the ocean surface. When the air gets that different from the sea, the dryness pulls moisture off little bumps in the ice, bits of ice vaporize, and the air gets humid — but only for a while. Question: Did ancient Greeks have a concept of nobility?
Answer: Absolutely. Originating from the Bronze Age, in both oligarch and democratic states, noble houses existed and were people of high status (In Athens, they were called “eupatridai”, meaning people with good fathers). The noble families boasted of their origin from the time of the heroes (the Mycenaean era) and some of them stretched it even further, claiming a divine origin. Take the royal family of Macedonia as an example, the Argeades. They claimed that Heracles was their forefather, whose father was Zeus. Although the hierarchy of the Mycenaean officials disappeared in the historical period, the surviving members of the noble houses took the leadership during the Archaic period with the conflict between them and the common but poor citizens never stopped. It brought violent uprisings and tyrannies but also fairer legislation and democracy. Did the nobles appreciate democracy? Most of them didn’t, this is why we have so many ancient authors criticizing democracy but they were loyal to the regime (most of the time…). Alcaeus the Mytilenian was a poet of the Archaic period (c. 600 BCE). He provides us with a good example of the attitude of the elite toward the people. The poetry of Alcaeus contains political fragments focusing on the emergence of tyranny. Alcaeus was anxious about Pittacus, a man of humble origin, rising to power, referring to the latter in disparaging terms. Alcaeus did not manage to stop Pittacus and was exiled. Nevertheless, Pittacus allowed him to return. As Pittacus was also listed as one of the Seven Sages of Greece, he could not have been all that bad… Pericles’ cup. The names of Pericles and five more members of his family are inscribed on this ceramic drinking cup. The most celebrated man of the Athenian democracy belonged (from his mother’s side) to the Alcmaeonides house, one of the most historical noble families of Athens.

Question: Was Medusa possibly the Minoan snake goddess?
Answer: This is a very interesting question in which…I can’t give a clear answer. Some academics (mostly in the early 20th century) claim there is a connection between the Minoan snake goddess and Medusa, the notorious mortal Gorgon of Greek mythology, with snakes and both protective powers as their connecting links. However, there are some dark spots. Snakes, which represent the cycles of life, the seasons, and immortality as it was thought to shed their skin indefinitely, appear in many Minoan artifacts as religious symbols but is the woman holding them a goddess? In the bronze figurine below, the woman with the (maybe) snakes on her head is a worshipper for sure as she is making the Minoan worship gesture of a facepalm. Minoan figurine, praying woman, 1600 – 1500 BC. Find from Troas, Asia Minor, Turkey. Antikensammlung Berlin, Ident. N. Misc. 8092, now in the Neues Museum Berlin. Image credit User:Zde - Wikimedia Commons To complicate things more, although the dominant theory wants the snake goddess as a kind of animal mistress connected with fertility and rebirth, there are different opinions on what the goddess represents with the discussion going on until now. Woman-bearing snakes disappeared for long from Greek art after the collapse of the Minoans. Before we meet the snakes-bearing Medusa, we find her in the 7th century BCE Theogony by Hesiod but…she is a monster and has no snakes! “And again, Ceto bore to Phorcys the fair-cheeked Graeae, sisters grey from their birth … and the Gorgons who dwell beyond glorious Ocean in the frontier land towards Night where are the clear-voiced Hesperides, Sthenno, and Euryale, and Medusa who suffered a woeful fate: she was mortal, but the two were undying and grew not old. With her lay the Dark-haired One [Poseidon] in a soft meadow amid spring flowers. And when Perseus cut off her head, there sprang forth great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus…” Hesiod, Theogony, In 270, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White In the art of the same period, known as the Orientalizing period, Medusa made her first appearance. She is a Centaurine in this Cycladic relief amphora of 650 BCE (no snakes) Paris Musée du Louvre CA 795. Photo. Chuzeville © Musée du Louvre The snakes make their appearance a little later while she’s still a monster Medusa wearing the belt of the intertwined snakes, a fertility symbol, as depicted on the west pediment of the Temple of Artemis on the island of Corfu. Dated ~580 BCE. Image Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International Are the symbols in common hard evidence to support the connection between the two? In addition, Medusa is also connected with Levantine deities (she was often depicted bearing wings), the Egyptian Eye of Horus, and the Egyptian snake goddess, Wadjet. So, she is primordial and predates the Greeks but her exact origin is still unclear. footnotes 57: Medusa Up Close and Personal From Snake Goddess to Medusa Medusa, Apollo, and the Great Mother on JSTOR Minoan snake goddess figurines - Wikipedia

Question: Are the Azore Islands the last remnants of ancient Atlantis?
Answer: Nah! The Azores islands are a complicated case in Geology. All nine of them are of volcanic origin because of the Azores hotspot. A hotspot is a column of upwelling hot magma which partially melts the crust and forms volcanoes. For extra fun, this hotspot is located at the meeting point of three tectonic plates, the North American plate, the European plate, and the African plate, the impressive Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The MAR is spreading and creating new oceanic crust, the Azores Plateau in our case. The location of the Azores Archipelago islands pointed to on either side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the Azores Plateau is highlighted in red. The Plateau was formed between 20 and 10 million years when the Azores hotspot and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading center were in roughly the same position. So, neither the structure nor the age of the islands point to a submerged continent. Sorry! footnotes The Azores Case Study Historia Natural de la Macaronesia

Name: Giota Detsi
Question: Were the Minoans and the Mycenaeans Greek? They were Minoans and Mycenaeans.
Answer: The question (which includes an answer too) is a bit of a trap question. It’s like asking, were the Aztecs and the Mayas Mexicans? So, the answer is “sort of”, as they used to live in the same area that is now called Greece and their successors are the Greeks of the historical and current days. If we travel back to 1600 BCE, we meet with the Mycenaeans on the mainland. These people (who didn’t call themselves Mycenaeans…) spoke Greek and had the same religion and many cultural elements as the Greeks of the historical period. We can easily identify them as the proto-Greeks. At the same time, the Minoans (who didn’t call themselves Minoans…) spoke a mysterious, not deciphered language and had a different religion. They were different people. But look what happened next. Circa 1450 BCE, the Mycenaeans conquered the Minoan Crete and then the two cultures started to merge. A lot of Minoan elements (such as religious games and administration system) were incorporated into the Mycenaean culture and, on the other hand, the Cretans started to write into the proto-Greek Linear B. The Bronze Age collapse (1171 BCE) stopped this procedure as both civilizations were destroyed. After the Bronze Age collapse, Crete’s and the mainland’s cultures homogenized into what we know as the Greek civilization. So, the Mycenaeans were definitely proto-Greeks. The Minoans were not initially but they turned into Greeks in the historical period. After all, Mycenaeans, Minoans, and Greeks share the same genetical origin.

Name: Giota Detsi
Question: Do we know what really caused the Bronze Age collapse or nah? Are these just theories that are widely agreed by historians? Do they have evidence or no? What really caused it is my question? Was it drought or anything?
Answer: Although we have strong evidence of events (caused both by nature and human activity) capable of bringing a collapse, I have to answer nah. A prolonged drought that lasted for centuries is well documented both by environmental archaeology and correspondence between the rulers of the period found in digs. There is also evidence of strong earthquake storms around the Aegean region. These natural disasters might not be enough to eliminate a regime but could be the cause of population movements (hunger and poverty can turn angels into demons!) such as the descent of the Dorians in Greece and the Sea Peoples or the increased aggression of the Mycenaeans. The Sea Peoples are referred to in Egyptian inscriptions as people coming (and) from the sea, bringing their families with them. They looked like belonging to more than one ethnicity but our knowledge about them is limited. Image File:Medinet Habu Ramses III. Tempel Nordostwand Abzeichnung 01.jpg - Wikimedia Commons This scene from the north wall of Medinet Habu is often used to illustrate the Egyptian campaign against the Sea Peoples during the reign of Ramesses III. The accompanying hieroglyphs do not name Egypt's enemies, describing them simply as being from "northern countries". At this point, assumptions and questions take the place of facts; we don’t know whether the raiders who destroyed the kingdom of Cyprus (Alasiya) and Ugarit were the same ones who tried to invade Egypt. The correspondence between the two kings found in the Ugarit archives shows that none of them was sure about the invaders’ identity. And what about the Mycenaeans’ military activity in Asia Minor, documented in the Hittite archives? Were they part of the Sea Peoples or did they operate independently? Or else? And why did their regime collapse too? This havoc, obviously, destroyed the Mediterranean commerce networks, depriving the palatial centers of the opportunity to cope with the shortage of food and the metalsmiths of bronze production. There is a profound connection between the drought, the raids, and the destroyed networks. However, we still can’t document sufficiently which was the vital cause of the simultaneous collapse of so many Bronze Age kingdoms. Maybe it was the combination of all the above, the perfect storm, who knows… footnotes 3.2 ka BP Megadrought and the Late Bronze Age Collapse Severe multi-year drought coincident with Hittite collapse around 1198–1196 bc - Nature Earthquake and the Catastrophic End of the Late Bronze Age in the Eastern Mediterranean https://www.researchgate.net/publication/301894299_The_%27Sea_Peoples%27_in_Primary_Sources The Alasiya-Correspondence The Hittite texts: Assuwa, Ahhiyawa, and Alaksandu of Wilusa https://www.mining.com/the-metals-of-antiquity-tin/

Question: What happened to the bodies of the 300 Spartans?
Answer: The usual for the dead warriors procedure was followed, they were buried in a tumulus on the Kolonos hill at Thermopylae. Aerial view of the battlefield. Location A is Kolonos hill, where the last of the Spartans fell and where the tumulus was found. Location B is the defensive wall constructed by the Phocaeans (it is referred to in Herodotus) and Γ is the spring in the Greek camp. Although the topography of the battlefield terrain is dramatically changed mainly due to sedimentation in the Malian Gulf (the old track appears at the foot of the hills around the plain, flanked by a modern road), the excavations conducted by Spyros Marinatos in 1939 were fruitful. He located the tumulus, only to be destroyed by the fortifications of the Hellenistic Age. He wrote in the press of the time: from the newspaper "ASSYRMATOS", on 06/17/1939 The excavations at Leonidas Hill are being completed. It is now certain that the extensive fortifications of the Hellenistic Age, which were carried out on the hill, have unfortunately destroyed the tomb of the heroic Three Hundred. Therefore, almost all of the findings come from the slopes of the hill, where the soils were decalcified when the top was flattened. However, among the latest finds are various copper plates, which come from the shattered armor of the heroes. Some bronze bells are of particular importance, because we can, based on a passage by Aeschylus, say with certainty that they come from the shields of the Spartans, which, at that time, were decorated with such bells. Also, the archaeological dig brought to light a silver cup, undoubtedly of Persian origin, because, according to the testimony of Herodotus, the Persians had an abundance of gold and silver cups, many of which we have found in the excavations carried out in Artemisium and Plataea. Although the topography and defense tactics at the Middle Pass of Thermopylae have been an issue of debate to our days, Marinatos’ reproduction seems the most faithful and best documented. A stone lion with the inscription of Simonides “Stranger, tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here, faithful to their laws” was erected at the hill to honor the Spartans (now lost). At the same spot, a modern monument is constructed The Monument of Thermopylae was constructed and erected at the expense of Greeks in America. Question: Is the archaeology of Troy about the ancient Greeks?
Answer: No, archaeology doesn’t work like this. The excavation leads to civilizations and people through the findings. The motto is “Let’s see what’s hidden under the hill”, not “Let’s find what the Greeks (replace the Greeks with the peoples you prefer) hide under the hill”. In the case of Troy, Schliemann followed the wrong path and was punished for it. In his quest for the Homeric Troy, he assumed that this should be the oldest Troy; it wasn’t. While he excavated brutally (he used dynamite!) the layers he believed were not of interest, he destroyed the Homeric city. So, the archaeology of Troy is about the inhabitants of the city and their civilization. Later more professional excavations proved it was a vibrant multi-cultured city during the Bronze Age and a Greek one during the historical period. If only Schliemann had followed the right motto… Reconstruction of Troy VI which might have been the Homeric city. Question: Why did Alexander the Great not conquer Sparta?
Answer: Alexander didn’t conquer any Greek city-state, why should he? Philip II, his father, created a Greek confederation allied against the Persians (the Corinthian League) in 340 BCE, with him being the military leader. Members of the alliance agreed never to attack each other except to suppress a revolt. Alexander inherited not only the Macedonian throne but the leadership of the Corinthian League too in which Sparta was not a member. He let it be as, just like his father, thought he had nothing to gain by forcing the Spartans to join the alliance. The alliance was strong enough without the Spartans who were too weak by then and incapable of becoming a serious threat. A note: Neither Philip nor Alexander conquered or occupied officially the city-states of the alliance. This changed later in the Hellenistic period. Alexander did take military action against Athens and Thebes because they revolted. Yet again, he didn’t enslave the cities.

Question: Will the expansion of the Universe continue to accelerate forever? If so, should it not eventually reach the rate of inflation?
Answer: For the moment, there is proof that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating pace thanks to the mysterious dark energy (we know what it does, but we don’t know what it is). However, physicists do expect it all to end at some point. What will happen next is under discussion with five main theories dominating the field. The Big Freeze (the most accepted model) suggests that if dark energy keeps accelerating the expansion of the universe forever (we have evidence of it) then the cosmos will die a slow death; the expanding universe will stretch the wavelength of the stars’ light farther and farther towards the red end of the spectrum. The expansion would dilute the dust and gas floating around in space until there isn’t enough concentrated in any one region to fuel the birth of new stars. With no more being born, stars eventually become an endangered and then extinct species, as the last of them die off. The white dwarfs, the neutron stars, the black dwarfs, and finally the black holes will follow and nothing else will ever happen. A diagram comparing the possible trajectories of the universe's expansion, towards either a Big Freeze/Rip model (red) or a Big Crunch (yellow) Royalty-free Images, Photo Stock, Video & Music | Depositphotos The Big Rip suggests that the dark energy accelerates the universe exponentially pushing more and more objects beyond the boundary limited by the speed of light ( the cosmic event horizon). These objects, unable to interact with gravitational or electromagnetic forces will eventually crumble starting from the biggest galaxies and ending to spacetime itself. The Big Crunch predicts a different procedure. Gravity will win its battle with dark energy and the universe will begin to contract until everything is crushed into a singularity (kind of reverse Big Bang). The Big Bounce is more optimistic; moments before the universe collapses into an infinitely dense singularity, it’s saved by quantum processes and reverses course once again, beginning a new period of expansion that’s effectively another Big Bang for a brand new universe. And, finally, the Big Slurp model suggests that a big “bubble” of false vacuum decay will expand engulfing everything; a system will naturally try to become stable. To do so it moves from a state of high energy to one with lower energy, until it stabilizes into its lowest possible energy state. For quantum fields, this is known as its vacuum state. All the known quantum fields are in their stable vacuum states – except for one: the Higgs field. It seems to be in a false vacuum state, which means that it currently appears stable but is predicted to not be in its lowest energy state. But that could change without warning. To put it more dramatically, the false vacuum bubble has just swallowed the Sun and will be here in eight minutes!

Question: How likely is a Carrington-like event? Should I be afraid of the Sun sending us and our lifestyle back to ancient times where cruel wars and occupations would be norm?
Answer: coronal mass ejection (CME). (Image credit: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center) Back in the last summer days of 1859 a lot of things happened at the same time; A powerful coronal mass ejection (CME) headed straight on Earth while a smaller CME erupted from the Sun in late August and effectively cleared the path between Earth and the Sun of most of the solar wind plasma that would normally slow down a CME. So, the conditions were perfect for the massive storm to race across the inner solar system and slam into Earth within just a few hours. And it did; voila the Carrington Event. Its results: Earth experienced an unprecedented geomagnetic storm, with telegraph systems going haywire and auroral displays — normally confined to polar latitudes — visible in the tropics. People in New England were able to read the newspaper in the middle of the night without any additional light. Meanwhile, in Colorado, miners believed it was daybreak and began their morning routine. However, the Carrington Event (like all CMEs) was completely harmless for human life. How likely is another Carrington Event? A study published on January 22, 2020, in Geophysical Research Letters from the University of Warwick on January 29, 2020, explained: This result was made possible by a new way of analyzing historical data … from the last 14 solar cycles, way before the space age began in 1957, instead of the last five solar cycles currently used. We find that on average there is a 4% chance of at least one … severe storm per year, and a 0.7% chance of a Carrington class storm per year … These super-storms are rare events but estimating their chance of occurrence is an important part of planning the level of mitigation needed to protect critical national infrastructure. However, a Carrington-class superstorm did erupt from the Sun on 23 July 2012 and narrowly missed Earth by just nine days, providing a stark warning from our solar parent that it is only a matter of time before another Carrington-class event impacts Earth, causing severe electrical disruptions, blackouts, and damages to electrical grids. This is what it means in layman’s terms: Electronic payment systems at grocery stores and gas stations would likely crash, electric vehicle charging stations — that rely on the power grid — would likely be unusable for some time, as would ATMs which rely on internet and/or satellite links to verify account and cash disbursement information. Television signals from satellites would be majorly disrupted, and satellites, too, would experience disruptions to radio frequency communication, crippling GPS navigation.. Planes flying over the oceans would likely experience navigation errors and communications blackouts as a result of the disrupted satellite network. Astronauts onboard space stations would either seek shelter in a radiation-hardened modul or, if enough time permitted and the CME event was significant enough, enter their return spacecraft and come home. Should we be afraid? There’s no need for panic. Unlike 1859, today, we have an international fleet — including the Solar Dynamics Orbiter, SOHO, the Parker Solar Probe, and the European Space Agency’s Solar Orbiter of vehicles constantly observing the Sun and seeking to understand the underlying mechanisms that generate sunspots, solar flares, and Coronal Mass Ejections, which while linked to one another do not automatically follow each other and can provide a multi-day warning that a CME has occurred and is heading toward Earth. Having a multi-day warning would give us time to shut down power stations and transformers, stop long-haul and transoceanic flights, and basically hunker down and wait for it to pass. However, the best we could do now is simply try to minimize the damage. So, we shouldn’t be afraid but we should be seriously concerned. further reading https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2023GL106632 How likely is another Carrington Event? | Earth | EarthSky The Carrington Event: History's greatest solar storm Wild solar weather is causing satellites to plummet from orbit. It's only going to get worse.

Question: Do we know where Oumuamua came from or where it originated from?
Answer: Oumuamua (messenger or scout in Hawaiian) is an object hurtling through our Solar System at an incredible speed, seemingly originating from interstellar space. The truth is we can only speculate what it is and where did it came from. Artistic representation of OUMUAMUA - mapcards.net Traditional comets and asteroids from within our solar system are relatively easy to categorize based on their composition and behavior. However, Oumuamua defied easy classification as its unusual shape, lack of a discernible coma or tail, and especially the rapid non-gravitational acceleration puzzles researchers. The non-gravitational Acceleration is its observed acceleration that cannot be solely explained by gravitational forces and results to a deviation from its expected trajectory (it is also responsible for the Interstellar craft assumption). The best theories so far: A hypothesis speculates that Oumuamua could be a fragment of a destroyed planet or exoplanetary system, ejected into interstellar space by a catastrophic event. This theory would explain its odd shape and unusual trajectory, as well as its lack of a coma or tail. There have been also suggestions that Oumuamua originated from the Pleiades star cluster. While the Pleiades is a well-known & beautiful cluster of stars, located ~ 444 light-years away in the constellation of Taurus there is currently no scientific evidence supporting this theory. It remains an intriguing but unproven idea in the realm of speculation. Astronomers haven't definitively detected any fully formed planets orbiting stars in the Pleiades yet. However, there is evidence that suggests planets are forming or have recently formed there. In 2007, researchers found evidence of dust clouds around a young star in the Pleiades called HD 23514. These dust clouds are thought to be the result of collisions between planet embryos, which are early stages of planets. This suggests that rocky planets, similar to those in our solar system, may be forming in the Pleiades. In sum, there is an abundance of theories and you know what this means; none of them is totally convincing. To unravel Oumuamua’s mysteries, astronomers are eager to detect and study more interstellar visitors in the future and telescopes promise to enhance our ability to observe & analyze objects like this strange object with greater precision. Question: What is the definitive proof of Earth revolves around the Sun, and not the other way around, or maybe both are revolving around each other?

Do you notice that all the planets of the solar system have phases (use the binoculars!)? That means that we look at them from different angles, we only see part of the illuminated half of them. The only way for this to happen is for the planets to orbit the sun. Attention! That doesn't mean the solar system has to be heliocentric. It's still possible that the Earth is at the center and the sun orbits the Earth but Venus orbits the sun. It would be weird—but it's possible. Now turn your binoculars to Saturn and its moons (you can see them!). What you see is that these moons are orbiting Jupiter and not the Earth. So, Earth isn't the center of everything. This means that the angular velocity for the planets decreases with orbital distance and the Earth orbits "faster" than Mars. Question: Are iron swords better than bronze swords?
Answer: Yes, they are. However, each of them has pros and cons. Bronze was always the favorite metal of the ancient metalsmiths. It was relatively easy to process and back in the Bronze Age, traders had their means to reach the tin needed in distant markets. Bronze is not perfect. It bends relatively easily and tends to dull more quickly, which is why shorter, stabbing daggers tended to be more practical during the Bronze Age. (a lot of the longer blades of the Mycenaean era tend to show signs of frequent repairs, especially around the area of the hilt, where they tended to break or split). But on the other hand, a lower temperature is needed for its procession—that the Bronze Age metalsmiths could acquire— copper was in abundance and easy to mine, and doesn’t rust. For these reasons, although iron was known during the Bronze Age, it was neglected. Naue II-type bronze sword. The most successful weapon of the Bronze Age. Image from The Naue II Sword - Bronze-Age-Craft The turbulence of the Bronze Age collapse made access to tin sources impossible (no tin no bronze), pure copper was too soft for weaponry, so iron (which was also in abundance) came in the first row when the main problem of its processing, the high melting temperature was finally solved. The first iron swords (c. 12 century BCE) were significantly different from later steel swords. They were work-hardened, rather than quench-hardened, which made them about the same or only slightly better in terms of strength and hardness than earlier bronze swords. This meant that they could still be bent out of shape during use. The easier production, however, and the greater availability of the raw material allowed for much larger-scale production. The Luristan sword is known as one of the earliest types of Iron Swords in History – Credits: Cerjak The further improvement of the iron process using quenching and tempering resulted in hard iron swords that could still be bent out of shape during use without breaking. Iron weapons were here to stay although bronze continued to be used for tools and artifacts. further reading and source Why Did it Take So Long Between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age? Iron vs Steel Swords: Structure, History, and Metal .

Question: Why did ancient civilizations use coins instead of paper money as a form of currency? Was paper money not available or practical at the time?

The Code of Hammurabi includes regulations for banking which was operated in temples, royal places, and private houses. Customers deposited their livestock, crops as well as precious stones. Despite their early status, these banks not only took deposits but also made loans and charged interest. Receipts came to the used for transfers not only to the original deposits but also to third parties. Receipt for clothes The system may sound genius but had some flaws as it was difficult to carry too many of these spacious, fragile receipts. It was also difficult to calculate an exchange rate, people needed something of standard value. So, silver became the standard of value sometime between 3100 BCE and 2500 BCE, along with barley. Silver was chosen because it was a prized decorative material, it was portable and the supply of it was relatively constant and predictable from year to year. The invention of coins (which means that a specific piece of metal was guaranteed by the state of its purity and weight) replaced all the other forms of currency, as it was the most portable and of known value. footnotes

Question: Do earthquakes have an equivalent for exoplanets?

This type of quake occurs on a planet with a dense atmosphere. The atmosphere causes the crust of the planet to expand and contract. The pressure changes when this happens, causing the crust to crack and rebound. If the cracks become too large, they can lead to a pulsating quake. 2. Rotational Quakes. A planet's rotation may cause its crust to bulge outwards. This creates tension between the upper and lower layers of the planet's crust. As the planet rotates, the stress increases until it becomes strong enough to rupture the rock. This leads to a rotational quake. 3. Tectonic Shaking. Tectonic shaking is similar to rotational oscillation except that it does not involve the entire planet. Instead, tectonic vibration only affects certain areas of the planet. It is believed that tectonic shaking occurs when two plates collide. One plate slides under another, creating friction. Friction heats the plates, which eventually breaks them apart. Once the plates separate, the resulting shock wave travels through the planet's mantle. 4. Volcanic Shaking. Volcanoes are one of the best ways for an object to lose heat. They create hot lava flows that travel through the planet's interior. When the lava hits the mantle, it produces a volcanic shake. 5. Crustal Shaking. Crustal shaking occurs when the top layer of the planet s crust moves relative to the underlying mantle. This movement causes the veil to vibrate, which results in a seismic event. That is, no matter where you are in the Universe, avoid tall buildings. footnotes

Question: Who built the Pharos of Alexandria?
Answer: I know what you mean, you want to know who built the lighthouse on Pharos of Alexandria! You see, Pharos (Greek name) is the islet located on the coastline of Alexandria which provides the only natural harbor there. Not convinced? This is a common misunderstanding but here’s what Homer wrote, centuries before the magnificent construction was made: In the 4th book of Odyssey, Menelaus referred to the island of Pharos and so did Herodotus in his “The Histories” II.112-120 (see the links for details). The story of the name Pharos, it’s a typical case of “lost in translation” (and rather funny): The king of Sparta Menelaus, on his way home after the Trojan War, went out to the island (this island), whose name he did not know. He asked a man who the owner was and what his name was, and he replied "Pera'a". Menelaus, however, paraphrased it to "Pharos" – which in ancient Greek means blanket (τὸ φᾶρος: cloth, wax) – and gave this name to the island and later to the lighthouse. The extra funny part is that the man’s reply was not about the island but that the owner was the pharaoh! The word Pharaoh originates from the word per-aa which means big house, palace and after paraphrasing, came to denote, metaphorically, the king. Lighthouse #3 is a photograph by Photo Researchers that was uploaded on March 14th, 2013. To go back to the lighthouse; was constructed by the architect Sostratus of Cnidos after an order from Ptolemy I Soter circa 300 BCE. It was ahead of its era in construction, being around 100 m in height, whose light could be seen at a distance of 7 miles at least, as a mirror was probably in use as Arab authors referred to later. Question: Do total solar eclipses occur elsewhere in the solar system?
Answer: A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes in front of the sun. We call it a total solar eclipse when the moon, Earth, and the Sun are aligned, and as our satellite passes between our planet and the Sun blocks completely the sunlight. As a satellite, a planet and the Sun are the only things needed for a solar eclipse, all the planets with a satellite system can have solar eclipses. For a total eclipse, more requirements are needed; the satellite must be big enough to hide the Sun completely and orbit the planet on the same plane as the sun. Phobos and Deimos, Mars’ satellites are too small to create a total eclipse, here is the best they can do: (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Malin Space Science Systems/Texas A&M University) The Mars rover Curiosity took these images of an annular, or ring, eclipse as Mars' largest moon, Phobos, passed directly in front of the sun on Aug. 20, 2013. The photos were taken 3 seconds apart. The gas giants, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, can all have total solar eclipses, as they have large moons and the sun appears small to them. In addition, the eclipses on them are frequent as they have numerous moons. Jupiter’s moon Io casts a shadow on the planet, creating a total eclipse, in this image taken by the Juno spacecraft on September 11, 2019. It is currently impossible to view the eclipse from the planet’s surface as there are no spacecraft flying close to it. The raw image was color-enhanced by citizen scientist Kevin M. Gill. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS/Kevin M. Gill) Sun is eclipsed by Saturn’s moon Titan, as seen by the spacecraft Cassini. On the lower right of the ring, one can also see Saturn’s moon Enceladus. Charon (Pluto's largest moon) is large enough and close enough to Pluto to produce total solar eclipses for Pluto.
