Question: What is the ultimate fate of the universe, and what will happen in the long-term?
Answer: There are not only one but five different theories about the end of the universe. They differ not only in the way the universe ends but also in the time of the collapse. In layman’s terms, this means we can’t predict with precision yet what will happen at the end. A diagram of the Big Bang, which would continue to expand forever in the Big Freeze model by Royalty-free Images, Photo Stock, Video & Music | Depositphotos The most likely scenario is the Big Freeze. If dark energy (dark energy is what causes the universe to accelerate; we know very little about it apart from the fact it exists) keeps accelerating the expansion of the universe forever – calculations suggest that it will – then the cosmos is in for a slow death that’s drawn out for googol years (10^100). In another model, dark energy (again!) doesn’t just accelerate the expansion of the universe at a steady pace, it accelerates exponentially, eventually tearing the very fabric of reality apart – an ending called the Big Rip. (estimated time 22 billion years) Or, perhaps the universe will end in the exact opposite way – instead of expanding forever into nothingness, it changes course and collapses in on itself in a so-called Big Crunch, like a reverse Big Bang. Eventually, the entire contents of the universe will be crushed together into an impossibly tiny space, a singularity. (estimated time a billion years). A diagram comparing the possible trajectories of the universe's expansion, towards either a Big Freeze/Rip model (red) or a Big Crunch (yellow) Royalty-free Images, Photo Stock, Video & Music | Depositphotos A variation on the above hypothesis suggests that moments before the universe collapses into an infinitely dense singularity, it’s saved by quantum processes and reverses course once again, beginning a new period of expansion that’s effectively another Big Bang for a brand new universe. This model is known as the Big Bounce. The last theory is the most spectacular and most terrifying. It is called the false vacuum decay or the Big Slurp. A system (universe is a system…) tries to become stable according to physics. To do so, it moves from a state of high energy to one with lower energy, until it stabilizes into its lowest possible energy state. For quantum fields, this is known as its vacuum state. It’s thought that all known quantum fields are in their stable vacuum states – except for one: the Higgs field. It seems to be in a false vacuum state, which means that it currently appears stable but is predicted to not be in its lowest energy state. But that could change without warning. Literally any second, the Higgs field could suddenly slip into a lower energy state, taking out a huge chunk (if not all) of the universe in the process. from The end of everything: 5 ways the universe could be destroyed

Question: Why didn't the ancient Greeks invent gravity?
Answer: Nobody has invented gravity. Gravity is the force, in a broader sense(*), of attraction between two or more masses anywhere in the Universe. It is a part of nature’s behavior which has existed before humanity and will be present after we’re gone. So, the ancient Greeks, or anyone else, couldn’t have invented it. However, the Greeks did try to explain it. Aristotle, for instance, claimed that objects fell towards the Earth because the Earth being the center of the Universe, attracted all of the mass in the Universe towards it (this claim has a tiny core of truth…) in Physics Book VIII. He also thought that the speed of a falling object should increase with its weight (this is completely wrong). In fact, they couldn’t do much better, they lacked the required mathematics. Newton, who actually studied gravity, had to invent it. (*) Space and time are not separate in the way we normally think, they are part of a combined concept called spacetime and, in addition, are not static. It changes (curves) in response to the presence of masses. This curving of spacetime is gravity. Question: What are some of the worst examples of the deliberate destruction of historical artifacts in history?

Greed is another enemy; Giuseppe Ferlini went to Sudan in 1830 seeking ancient treasures. So, meet Michel Fourmont (a French antiquarian, classic scholar, and member of the Academie des Inscriptions. This man is notorious for the destruction of the antiquities in ancient Sparta and having presented as genuine some forged inscriptions. These are his own words, in a letter to Bignon (1730): For more than a month, although ill, I am working with 30 laborers for the complete destruction of Sparta; hardly a day goes by without finding something, and some days have produced as many as 20 inscriptions. If I could do at Tegea, Antigonia (Mantineia), Nemea and one or two other cities what I have done at Hermione, Troezen, and Sparta, it wouldn't be necessary to send anyone here. There would be nothing left. I have not been able to knock down the remains of the former places, because of the plague, without which they would be totally destroyed. For lack of books, these destructions shall be the only way to make illustrious a voyage which has caused such a stir Speaking frankly, I myself am astonished at this expedition. I have read nowhere that, since the restoration of literature, anyone has had the idea of turning whole cities upside down to find these marbles, which are the only irreproachable evidence of antiquity, the only things capable of shedding light on the dark corners of history, of the administration and religion of ancient peoples. Only in this manner can one contribute usefully to science. So convinced am I that Sparta is the fifth city of the Morea I have destroyed. Hermione and Troezen have had the same fate. I have not spared Argos, Philasia, and some others. I am currently working to dismantle the temple of Amyclean Apollo down to the foundation stone. Every day one finds things you will be pleased to see. ... I would destroy others with the same ease if I were left to do so The only thing I can say is, Lord, protect me from my enemies and from those who love me… footnotes Michel Fourmont - Wikipedia Buddhas of Bamiyan - Wikipedia Nubian pyramids - Wikipedia

Question: Did Middle Eastern Civilizations like Phoenicians & Egyptian had any influence on the early Minoans, Mycenaeans of Greece, the Etruscans & Latial culture/proto Romans during the Orientalizing period?
Answer: Wow, you ask a lot about a lot of people! I’ll take them one by one, right? The Minoan civilization of the Bronze Age predated the Phoenicians and, of course, had no influence by them. It also seems that the Egyptians, despite the general impression, had little influence too. The early Minoan culture (that is from 3,000 BCE to 2,000 BCE) was far from the mesmerizing civilization we meet in the next millennium; there are no palatial centers yet. The main "allies" and commercial partners of the Cretans during this period are the Cycladians and the Anatolians, as was the case since around 7000 BCE. Moreover, the last settlers came from there around 4,000 BCE, bringing with them the art of metallurgy, the cultivation of vineyards and olive trees, beekeeping, and other practices that the Minoans later developed in their own way. With Egypt, there were mainly trade transactions involving raw materials. (There is Egyptian influence later in architecture and the use of the column, but not in this early phase of the Minoan civilization). I think you’ll agree that the archaeological findings of this period shown below are convincing. Ewer from Crete, 2,500 BCE Cycladic type figurine from (Egyptian) ivory. Prepalatial period 2500–2300 BCE. All images are copyright of the Hellenic Ministry of Culture, via https://www.latsis-foundation.org/content/elib/book_12/heraklion_en.pdf The Mycenaean civilization (the merge of the Proto-Helladic civilization and the newcomers from the Caucasian steppes c. 2,000 BCE) had also different partners; the Minoans (mostly) and the Anatolians had the most influence on their art and technology. Truth be told, the references of many Greek myths to Egypt and the similarity to Egyptian ones of others reveal a strong cultural influence. The Orientalizing period (~700 BCE) finds the early Etruscan art already influenced by the Greeks. So, they followed them in adding Anatolian elements to their items ( lions, leopards, and mythological composite creatures such as sphinxes and griffins). The Phoenicians (who were influenced by the Egyptians…) had a say in this as they had interactions with both Etruscans and Greeks. Etruscan Chimera of Arezzo. Question: What process took city states from monarchy to aristocracy and in Athens to democracy?
Answer: There is not an easy or definite answer to this question as we lack evidence for crucial periods and events. At least, I’ll try to make my answer short, following the evolution of the Greek regimes step by step beginning from the Bronze Age and the proto-Greeks, the Mycenaeans. Step 1: The Mycenaean monarchy was not a strict monarchy; true, there was a king (the wanax) but the damos (the people’s assembly) is referred to in the Linear B tablets as having some limited power (eg., the land belonged to the state and the wanax couldn’t use it unless the damos’ decided on it). It is clear that even in the Bronze Age, the citizens participated (or at least, were present) in the decision-making of the state. Around 1100 BCE, this regime vanished. Evidence of riots is found, the wanax perished, and many members of the nobility fled away. Vouleutirion (assembly place, “parliament”) from pre-historic Poliochni, Lemnos. Image from Photos of Poliochni Lemnos Step 2: The dim Geometric period; still one leader, a king (c.1100-700 BCE) And now what, after the distraction of the Mycenaeans? Truth be told, we don’t know much. In this early Greek period, the lack of writing cost us a lot. The archaeological findings show the formation of the city-states as we know them. They are governed by one leader, most probably, the successors of the Mycenaean local governors, the vasileus, a king. We can only assume, judging from the Homeric epics, writings by later ancient authors, and tradition that the institution of the damos (demos from now on) kept on and the noble families (remnants of the Mycenaean years) formed a consulting group, the gerousia. Step 3: Aristocracy, the nobles get the power From this time point, each city-state took a different path; some, like Sparta and Macedonia, kept the kingship whereas others, the majority, proceeded with more reforms. In most cities the power of the king is limited gradually, leading to its abolition, mainly restricted by the desire of other members of noble and wealthy families to have a share in power. In Corinth, eg., it became an annual kingship first, limited to members of this lineage. That is, instead of the king holding his office for life, there is a rotation of members of this specific family in the position of the king. In the case of Athens, c. 752/1 BCE, the lifelong kingship abolished and is replaced by rulers with a ten-year term, who, however, came from the royal lineage. The ten-year rule of the king becomes an annual magistracy (682 BCE), and gradually, nine offices are created. One of them is the Archon Basileus, a remnant of royal office, even only by name. Aristocracy (=the power to the nobles) had emerged. More institutions of authority are established, such as the voule (parliament) and the Areopagus. All members are still aristocrats but have to be elected. In this period, one more revolutionary event happened; the Greeks started to write again. Among the first texts were the laws of each city. Written on public walls, they were accessible to every citizen. Although the first laws concerned mostly family, inheritance, and economic rights, they indirectly affected the political system, as they determined when a resident of the city was simultaneously a citizen (differences exist from city to city). In addition, being written in public and known to all somewhat limited the predatory disposition of the nobles. The law of Dreros is the earliest recorded European law (650–600 BCE). Image credit the Constitutional Law of Dreros: The Earliest Surviving Greek Law on Stone Although ten aristocrats (instead of one) were in charge and happy about it, the middle class and, mainly, the farmers were furious with the administration; the financially struggling among them lost their farms and even their freedom due to debts. As if that weren't enough, complaints about injustices against the weak were numerous (the references to by Hesiod are characteristic). Step 4: Democracy Some city-states attempted to alleviate the explosive situation through colonies. Others, like Athens, proceeded with reforms mainly focusing on the economic and legal framework of each class. However, inevitably, political rights were granted to the middle and lower class for the first time (~600 BCE). A note: That wasn’t out of courtesy; in ancient Greece, citizenship was tightly related to the ability to be under arms. As the Athenian soldiers paid for their armor themselves, whoever participated in the army (the middle class) demanded more political rights. Gradually, as more and more Athenians joined the army, all were granted full rights c.460 BCE, meaning that all the Athenians could be elected and vote, no matter their financial status or their family’s origin. The recent Persian Wars and the oncoming clash with Sparta convinced everyone that the military power, and therefore the entirety of the Athenian citizens, had to be as strong as possible. EDIT: Democracy was not a miracle, as it didn’t happen suddenly nor is inexplicable. However, an attempt to follow all the events one by one in detail (and explain their cause) would make this answer extremely long and I may say extremely boring. So, I chose to write a very brief summary, avoiding dates and names…

Question: How does NASA study exoplanets (planets outside our solar system), and what have been some notable discoveries?
Answer: An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system orbiting other stars, but there are also free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, that orbit the galactic center and are untethered to any star. The first exoplanet, 51 Pegasi b, was discovered in 1995 by NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope. It is a hot, star-hugging gas giant believed to be about half the size of Jupiter. It tugged so hard on its parent star as it raced around in a four-day orbit that the star’s wobbling (keep this…) was obvious to earthly telescopes. Now, astronomers knew what to look for. 51 Pegasi b, also called "Dimidium," was the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a star like our sun. This groundbreaking find in 1995 confirmed planets like Earth could exist elsewhere in the universe. Credit: NASA (artistic presentation) A statistical estimate based on data from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope revealed that there are more planets than stars in our galaxy. That means there are more than a trillion planets in our galaxy alone, many of them in Earth’s size range. Up to now, more than 5,000 exoplanets have been discovered. How do we look for them? By reading the wobble of a star, that is, the change in its radial velocity; the wavelengths of starlight may appear alternately squeezed and stretched as a star moves slightly closer, then slightly farther away from us. Those gyrations are caused by gravitational tugs, this way and that, from orbiting planets. Then, spectroscopy is used to reveal the composition of the exoplanet. The color bands of its spectrum can be read like a bar code, revealing which molecules are present. Transit spectroscopy (light from a star travels through the atmosphere of an orbiting planet and reaches our telescopes) tells about where it's been. Gravitational microlensing takes advantage of an effect first described by Einstein: gravity's ability to warp and bend starlight. The gravity of a star in the foreground will magnify the light from a background star that passes just behind it. If the foreground star has a planet in orbit, the star will appear to a properly positioned telescope as a spike in light intensity as the background star goes by; the planet will appear as a second, smaller spike. Direct imaging, now available only for giant planets, it will be the next best thing…. A team of French astronomers used the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope to discover a giant exoplanet, Beta Pictoris b, resulting in this iconic direct image. Image credit: ESO/A.-M. Lagrange et al. Some notable discoveries: WASP-107b, a gas giant, orbiting a highly active K-type star about 200 light-years from Earth. Using spectroscopy, scientists detected helium escaping from the planet — the first time this element was found in an exoplanet atmosphere. Image credit: ESA/Hubble, NASA, M. Kornmesser Proxima Centauri b is our closest known exoplanet neighbor, at only 4 light-years away. It was discovered in 2016. Artistic impression via https://aminoapps.com/c/space/page/blog/proxima-centauri-b/g0gl_GxXU6uVwga0rY7VaoeQdJXYKVdWVbq Artist’s impression of CFBDSIR2149, the rogue planet wandering through space roughly 100 light years from our solar system (Image: ESO/L. Calçada/P. Delorme/Nick Risinger (Nick Risinger)/R. Saito/VVV Consortium). Discovered in 2012, it is the first rogue planet found. footnotes: How We Find and Characterize | Discovery – Exoplanet Exploration: Planets Beyond our Solar System

Name: Giota Detsi
Question: Did ancient Greeks have any awareness of other civilizations, such as the Minoan civilization of Crete, the Etruscans, or the Phoenicians?
Answer: Sure, the Greeks remembered the Minoans and interacted with both Etruscans and Phoenicians. The Minoans, a mesmerizing civilization of the Bronze Age, predated the Greeks and didn’t coincide with them. They had merged with the Mycenaeans (the proto-Greeks) since ~1450 BCE and a lot of myths referring to Minoans are found in Greek literature (unfortunately, no historical archives survived). However, the myths about the powerful King Minos, the Minotaur, and Daedalus (to refer to the most well-known) give us a glimpse of the events of prehistory as they hide a historical core for sure. The Greek authors of the classical period and beyond (Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato) wrote also about them, revealing the admiration of the Greeks and the hint that the Minoans had inspired the Spartan law. Although these claims were based only on the oral traditions, later archaeological evidence seems to verify it. The Etruscans lived in modern Tuscany, Italy during the historical period when the Greeks had already established colonies in Sicily and Southern Italy and had cultural and commercial interconnections. Here are some facts: The largest collection of attic vases is found in Italy as the exports to Etruscans were vast. Some pottery workshops in Athens exported their whole production to Etruria. This painting is from an Etruscan crater(~360 BCE) despite it looks very Greek. It is displayed in the Louvre. Image credit User:Jastrow - Wikimedia Commons A lot of Greek inscriptions are found in Etruscan territory, some dated back to the 8th c. BCE. The merchants of the Greek colonies were supplied iron from the island of Elba, and the mineral-rich areas of northern Etruria. There was some fuss about the Tyrrenian (the Etruscans in Greek) pirates but piracy was a common phenomenon back then. So, no big deal… The Phoenicians were the people that the Greeks respected the most (apart from the Egyptians). They gave them credit for their writing system and the many references to them in Greek mythology also reveal their gratitude as it was the Phoenicians who assisted (through trade) the Greeks to stand to their feet after the Bronze Age collapse. Of course, later on, they clashed for supremacy in the markets, but ultimately, space was found for both (The Phoenicians were more active in the West Mediterranean and the Greeks in the East). The peoples of the Mediterranean were and are 'condemned' to live together. They have always known each other and always had a kind of delicate balance in their relationships. Well, not always…

Question: Were the Minoans the same as Plato's Atlanteans? Making the island of Thera pre-volcanic eruption ~1,600BC a potential historical Atlantis? And were the Trojans further North related to the Minoans, culturally and/or linguistically?
Answer: Definitely not. image from Allegorical Atlantis by let-s-talk-about-myths-baby-merch Plato, like all writers, had the right to create allegories to highlight his views. The imaginary story of Atlantis served to point out to the arrogant Athenians what arrogance might bring to a state, nothing more was hidden in it. In addition, Plato most probably was not aware of the cataclysmic event of the 17th c. BCE. Doesn’t occur to you that although a lot of Greek myths referred to the Minoans (and most of them had a historical core) none of them referred to the eruption? Is it a paradox? Certainly not, there is an explanation. As we know, the Greeks kept in their collective memory as myths the events that had an impact on them; the Trojan War, the Argonauts, and the Minotaur are stories in which the Mycenaean Greeks were involved. Question: Mycenean Pylos was some kilometers inland, near the modern village of Choros (Modern Pylos is at the Ionian sea coast). Was the coastline further to the east in Mycenaean times?
Answer: It was not. Pylos was inland back then as it is today. As you can see in the map, the change in the coastline is insignificant although the region is close to the very active seismic Ionian arc. The few alterations were made by the Mycenaeans themselves because they had to construct a port. A very special, distinguished port… The coastline of W. Messenia now. See the lagoon North of the Navarino Bay? The Osman Aga (or Divari) lagoon was once the port of Pylos as you can see in the map below; The Bronze Age Pylos was built inland on the hill of Englianos, at a distance of approx. 5 km from the coast, following the Mycenaean rule for the major cities; they had to be on a hill so that they could have a good view of their land and protection from raids (the latter didn’t end well…). Being a major export center for olive oil and mainly aromatic oils, a port was needed. Here’s what they constructed: The river Sellas, navigable back then, was their route to the sea. It passed by the palatial center and they diverted it so that it could meet the sea at the port. The Pyleans loaded their goods onto boats, sailed down the river, crossed the artificial lake, and finally reached the port through a narrow passage. Why on Earth did they dig a lake? The port was next to dunes (Homer named the city sandy Pylos). The seawater continually carried sand that blocked the port and so did the sediment carried down by the river. That's where the lake came in; it functioned as a filter, as the river's gravel settled at the bottom of the lake, and the clean water that continued its flow cleared the mouth of the harbor too. This brilliant construction fell out of use by the end of the Bronze Age. The sediment and the sand transformed the ingenious construction to the beach below. Question: Do all Greek statues have small stature?
Answer: As sculpture was one of the main artistic expressions of the Greek culture and the culture covered almost a millennium, it is easily understood that it evolved more than once during this period. (A note: I won’t refer to statuettes in this answer.) From the very beginning, the Greek statues may depict both gods and humans and were often oversized, sometimes gigantic. Look eg., at this archaic kouros (actually, a burial mark, depicting the diceased man) from Samos: image from Login • Instagram As the Greeks entered the classical period, there was a change: human size for humans (still, you can’t call it small) and slightly oversized for deities. The Charioteer in Delphi (dated 478–474 BCE) is 1.80 m tall (human height) while Poseidon of Artemision (a god) is 2.09 m, too tall for a man. image from 317 Artemision Images, Stock Photos, 3D objects, & Vectors | Shutterstock In this period, a god’s height could be enormous, like the statues of Athena and Zeus by Pheidias (all gone). Athena Promachos, eg, (Athena who fights in the front line) was a colossal bronze statue that stood on the Acropolis of Athens. Her height was ~ 9 m. In the Hellenistic period, when harmony and metron were lost, even statues of humans (kings, for instance) could be seriously oversized. So, the Greek sculpture produced a lot of oversized artifacts (in any case, not small) during all periods. The truth is that excessive size wasn’t needed. The emphasis was always on the spirituality of the art.

Question: What was bathing like in Ancient Rome or Greece?
Answer: Personal hygiene was a serious matter for both Greeks and Romans (I can say they were bathing freaks…) and cleansing themselves was more than a ritual. They might bathe at home, in their bathtub, in their bathroom. This is an image from ancient Olynthos (it was destroyed and abandoned in 318 BCE). The children look at an ancient bath. The bath might be a clay-made seated bath (like in the image above) or a basin made of clay or marble (like below). Three young women bathing. Side B from an Attic red-figure stamnos, 440/30 BC. Accession number Inv. 2411, Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich, Germany Treatments with aromatic oils and beauty products for women would follow (a manicure and pedicure were necessary). image from Pinterest A shower was an option too image from Hellenica World Hot water or cold water? That depends on who you ask. The Spartans and the Macedonians preferred the cold ones as they believed that hot baths caused softness. The Athenians on the other hand, used hot and cold baths, which they considered a factor of health and culture. What about soap? The Greeks didn’t use soap. However, they had an effective cleansing method. They rub their body with ash and oils (the potassium of the ash and the oil make a natural soap) and then scrub it with pumice. Using a strigil (stleggis in Greek) they removed the remains of oil and ash and then doused them with water. Finally, they rub down with oil. a strigil of the classic period http://MetMuseum.com They could also take their bath in public facilities, the valaneia. The oldest ones we know of operated in Sybaris, an ancient city of Magna Graecia in southern Italy, at the end of the 6th century BCE. The valaneia appeared in Athens in the 5th century BCE, but their spread continued to be great during the Hellenistic period. The public baths could be of public or private ownership and were usually built close to gymnasiums. Athletes' baths in Nemea Bathing was also an important part of medical treatment. Hippocrates was the first to systematically study the therapeutic use of hot and cold baths and dissociate it from religion. He classified the waters into three categories: drinking water, salty water, and seawater. By "salty water" he meant thermal waters. The Romans continued and improved the use of public baths. The Roman public baths (the thermae) were used both for personal hygiene and socialization. They could be truly luxurious! Thermae from the city of Herculaneum A Roman would go first to the calidarium (warm pool), before moving on to the tepidarium (lukewarm pool) and frigidarium (cold pool). Finally, they will swim in the natatium, which is an outdoor pool. To ensure the hygiene of the facility, the architects of the baths planned the flow of water through and through the hot and cold basins. The necessary thousands of cubic meters of water were provided by aqueducts. Water will flow into a large tank in the main building where a distribution system either brings water to the cold pools or over wood burning for the use of hot and hot baths. In terms of drainage, the floor of each room led to the drains that ran down the distribution pipes to direct water to the municipal drainage system. A hypocaust from Cyprus (where a log fire heated elevated marble floors, channeling hot air through pipes in the wall, raised the temperature to over 210 degrees F. Bathers had to wear special shoes to protect their feet). If we think of it, a few things are added today…right? Question: What makes the Pergamon Ancient Greek Theatre unique, and what is its seating capacity and angle, distinguishing it in history?
Answer: It is a Hellenistic theatre, built on the steep west slope of the upper Acropolis of Pergamon. It was constructed in the 3rd century BCE, at the beginning of the Attalid dynasty, and renovated extensively by King Eumenes II (97-159 BCE). A marble stage house, a royal box, and a 246.5 meter-long, 17.4 meter-wide Doric colonnaded terrace (where the path is visible on the right of the photo below), the longest stoa in the Hellenistic world, were added later. The theater and a Byzantine tower. Image from Acropolis theatre of Pergamon The theatre may have had a seating capacity of 10,000 (the exact estimation is not possible) and the cavea (seating area) was the steepest in the ancient world (~70 degrees). The 80 rows of seats were arranged on three levels, divided by 3 walkways (diazomata) around the width of the cavea. At the front of the second row in the center of the cavea are the remains of the royal box. the royal box, image from Acropolis theatre of Pergamon The orchestra (stage) was a wooden construction that could be removed when not in use, to clear the terrace and the approach to the Temple of Dionysus at its north end. Today, all that remains of the monumental terrace is a footpath (on the right of the photo above), along which lie some of the fragments of the stoa (colonnade). It was replaced by a marble one in the 1st century BCE. Due to the limitations of the steep hillside site, the cavea could not be built wider than a semi-circle as in other Greek theatres, making the construction unique in the Hellenistic world. It was extended upwards to 37 meters above the orchestra and it was wise to watch your step…. footnotes Acropolis theatre of Pergamon ancient theatre of Pergamon

Question: How did we transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age?
Answer: Each region of the world has a different story to narrate. The most dramatic is the one of the Eastern Mediterranean region, the famous Bronze Age collapse. It happened circa 1100 BCE, when natural disasters, climate anomalies, and raids and riots destroyed commerce (whole kingdoms such as the Hittite and the Mycenaean perished). Tin, the main material for bronze apart from copper, couldn’t reach the region anymore so people were forced to turn to iron as a substitute. Truth be told, iron was known way before the collapse. However, technical difficulties in its process such as the high temperature required to melt and the complex procedure of removing impurities didn’t allow the Bronze Age people to produce an iron alloy with better properties than bronze’s. However, after the collapse, people in the Near East were forced to work with the available materials, such as iron, and quickly, solutions were found. Next-generation furnaces and the addition of carbon to the metal led to the mass production of early steel. Iron dagger from the Danube River Valley (Black Sea Region) dated in the 7th-6th century BCE. Image credit: XTREMELY RARE EUROPEAN SCYTHIAN ANCIENT IRON AKINAKES SHORT SWORD FROM THE BLACK SEA REGION *SC04 An interesting note: When trade was restored, bronze returned to the lives of people. It was always more popular than iron. One after the other, the neighboring civilizations, the Villanonans in Italy and the Northern Europeans (already good metal smiths) adapted the new material although without the drama of the Aegean region. In India, iron was been used as early as the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE. Artifacts including small knives and blades have been discovered dated between 2,400 BCE and 1800 BCE, making the Indians the pioneers of the use of iron. Question: How does "The School of Athens" contribute to our understanding of Renaissance art and its relationship to classical philosophy?
Answer: School of Athens, Raphael, 1508-1512, Vatican Museum, Rome This big (8m x 4m) emblematic painting of the early Renaissance had an impact like few others, affecting both the aesthetic and philosophical approach of Renaissance painters. The depiction is purely secular (not a single saint or religious symbol is present in the painting), despite being commissioned by the Pope in an attempt to elevate the Church's authority in the tumultuous early years of the Renaissance. The brilliant Raphael uses allegories extensively (for example, the iconic staircase of the school symbolizing the step-by-step progress of science and the 'confrontation' of Plato with Aristotle representing the two different approaches in philosophy - the realistic, naturalistic one of Aristotle against the idealism of Plato). Of course, to appreciate and understand the allegories, knowledge of science, philosophy, and the lifestyle of classical antiquity is necessary. It seems that the intended audience was knowledgeable, and the painter was aware of it. However, do not expect historical accuracy in the painting; it does not exist. Many of those depicted (such as Euclid, Pythagoras, Ptolemy, or Hypatia) never set foot in Athens and certainly were never members of the School of Athens. But the artist's goal is not that anyway. The goal (to integrate pagan philosophers into the framework of Christianity) is fully achieved, simultaneously creating an aesthetic masterpiece. for more details about the painting:

Question: What happened to the Minoans after they left Crete? Did they leave or get assimilated by other Greeks/Minoans? What happened to them in general afterwards (if anything)?
Answer: The Minoans never left their island en masse. They stayed there after the disaster from the Thera eruption and rebuilt their cities and economy. They stayed on their island even when it was conquered by the Mycenaeans. However, some moved to mountainous, isolated areas of the island in an attempt to avoid contact with the invaders. There are indications of Minoans migrating to Canaan after the Bronze Age collapse, but it seems to have been only a small group of refugees and not a massive migration as their genetic imprint disappeared completely in a relatively short period. The possible Minoan migration is under discussion as the genetic material shows Mediterranean people in general and the archaeological findings seem more Mycenaean than Minoan. Minoan Frescoes at Tel Kabri So, what happened to the Cretans? They quickly assimilated with the Mycenaeans (there are no indications of uprising or resistance). Although the administration shifted to the invaders, the Cretans continued to live in the same way with the same traditions. They stopped writing in Linear A and adopted (or, maybe, created) the Linear B writing system used by the Mycenaeans. (This is good news because the Linear B tablets found on Crete gave us valuable information about them). The destruction at the end of the Bronze Age marked the end of the common Minoan-Mycenaean civilization. The Cretans were now Greeks just like the Mycenaeans. They spoke Greek, worshipped the Olympian gods, and participated in the Panhellenic games. Minoan contributions are detected in the Greek culture; the religious games, the Eleusinian mysteries,and the Cretan’s only priests in the oracle of Delphi are only some examples. In the Homeric epics, which reflect the relations between the Greeks of the Geometric period, the Cretans seemed to be in perfect harmony with the rest of the Greeks. Geometric period pottery from Crete with Minoan elements Geometric Period - Gallery However, some elements of their old culture never died. For instance, they were the pioneers in law-making among the Greeks, were the best archers and acrobats and their art kept a lot of Minoan motives. A civilization of such class cannot vanish completely, can it? footnotes Popular Archeology - Archaeologists Uncover Rare Finds at an Ancient Canaanite Center Geometric and Archaic Period of Crete

Question: What is Ampheion in ancient Greece Thebes?
Answer: Ampheion is one of the most intriguing, controversial, and fascinating monuments of Greek antiquity. It is a tumulus associated with the two sons of Zeus, Zethos and Amphion, who walled Cadmeia, while from the name of Zethos' wife, Thebe, the city was renamed Thebes. The two brothers, according to myths, were buried in a common tomb, located in the northern part of Cadmeia, just outside the "Northern Gates", in a tomb, where according to Pausanias ("Boeotika" 17.4) "earth is the soil of the great". image from Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” image credit Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES A lot of ancient authors referred to the monument such as Xenophon in “Ellinika”, 5:48, Plutarch in “On the Demon of Socrates”, 4, and more. It was a well-known and well-respected monument during antiquity (it wasn’t looted or disturbed by any means until the early Christian years) and detailed descriptions of the monument and its position survived to our days. Ok, it’s a monument connected with mythological heroes, why is it intriguing, controversial, and fascinating? Its shape! image credit Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES It is a mastaba-type stepped pyramidoid with three levels (8.8. 4.4. and 2.2m respectively). Isn’t it fascinating? image from Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” A twin tomb on the top step! On top of the stepped pyramid was found a stone-built tomb which hosted two burials, confirming Pausanias’ words “εν κοινώ” (together). The box-shaped (2.20 x 1.15 meters) tomb consisted of large carved limestone slabs. The excavations brought to light other important items: skeleton remains and gold jewelry that escaped the robbers. image credit Bronze Age - MUSEUM OF THEBES OMG! Is it that old? The technique of the jewelry and the fragments of pottery found, date the burial in the Proto-Helladic (before the Mycenaeans) period ~2,500 BCE. That means that a story that old survived from the Mycenaean era until our days through the ancient authors. How much of the story is true (if any) we can’t tell but is certainly intriguing! More information about the monument. The monument was discovered in 1971 by the archaeologist Theodoros Spyropoulos. He also discovered a vast net of underground corridors under the monument but he was forced to close the dig before even photographing them. Until today, the corridors have not been explored thoroughly. However, the short emergency excavation carried out by the 7th Ephorate of Prehistoric and Classical Antiquities in 2007, immediately below the tumulus, discovered three chamber tombs dug into the natural rock of the hill, as well as a shallow carved grave for a woman with a baby in her arms. The tumulus is accessible although in bad condition. According to the ancient tradition, the inhabitants of the nearby Tithorea in Phocis secretly took soil from Amphion when the sun passed through the constellation Taurus (May). Pausanias says ("Boeotika", 17.4): "The sun conducted him in the heavens". The Tithorians, secretly taking soil from Amphio, brought it to the tomb of Antiope, the mother of the Thebans Dioskouri, and thus their country became more fertile, while the fertility of the Theban land decreased. footnotes Το Θηβαϊκό “Αμφείον” ������� �������� ������� Amfeio - MUSEUM OF THEBES

If you were more specific, it would be helpful… Part 1: The possible false narrative A lot of debunked-by-now stories involving the Minoans were (and maybe are…) believed by many for a simple cause: the storyteller was Sir Arthur Evans, the prominent archaeologist who practically unearthed Knossos (although he was not the first excavator). Evans spent decades digging, studying, and restoring his findings in Crete, and as expected, he was rightfully considered an authority on Minoan civilization. Some of his conclusions though, seem to be wrong: The dark-colored males deceived Evans. The truth is that males were depicted as dark to distinguish them from women. That also means that Minoans and Phoenicians were not genetically connected. Based on the colorful and peaceful frescos, the poor findings of weapons, and ignoring the fortifications he had unearthed, he concluded that the Minoans were peaceful, happy people. In addition, the evidence of human sacrifices indicates a population that had their fears and insecurities like everybody else during the Bronze Age. Evans was misled on purpose for two reasons; *reason one* the archaeophile audience was focused on the Aegean region after the discovery of Troy and the excavations at Mycenae. However, the Mycenaeans were a civilization of warriors and * reason two* their world was so similar to the situation in Europe in the early 20th century. Evans wanted to present to the world a different, peaceful, cheerful European civilization to contrast the Mycenaeans of Schliemann and give a motive to his contemporaries. (Note: We shouldn’t blame Sir Arthur Evans. He had done a tremendous job in Crete and despite some few mistakes, his essays on the Minoans are still considered valuable.) As the Minoans and Mycenaeans merged after the conquest of Crete by the latter, the Greeks retained genetic and cultural elements from both. Genetically, Greeks and Minoans are very close. Culturally, despite the Minoan loans the Greek civilization is way different. The Minoans predated the Phoenicians as well and the same genetic studies mentioned above show no connection between the two. The two people had commercial interactions and the Phoenicians “inherited” the trade routes after the Bronze Age collapse and the loss of the Minoan fleet. Question: How have earrings evolved in terms of cultural significance and style across different civilizations and time periods?
Answer: Earrings! If you’re a chic woman you adore them. If you’re a history lover, you adore them too because earrings are one of the oldest forms of jewelry, and evidence of their use can be traced back to ancient cultures all over the world. Otzi the Iceman, a mummified body found in the Italian Alpes 5,000 after his death, had pierced holes on his earlobes suggesting that earrings may have been worn for both aesthetic and cultural reasons. The oldest gold earrings unearthed are dated a little later, around 2600-2450 BCE. They belonged to Puabi, a Queen of Ur. Apart from the aesthetic value, earrings in Mesopotamia appeared to also hold spiritual significance. Puabi’s set of earrings. Image credit Collections - Penn Museum The Egyptians believed in the magical powers of jewelry. They believed that jewels could protect, heal, and bring luck to them, so, everybody wore a piece. Women, men, and probably children all used to wear earrings judging from the pieces found in tombs. In ancient Greece and Rome, earrings became a woman’s only accessory as they were connected with the worship of Aphrodite. They indicated a woman’s social status, therefore, the wealthier the lady the larger and more ornate the earrings. Look at how elaborate this 5 cm long pair from 300 BCE is; image credit Gold earrings with disk and boat-shaped pendant | East Greek | Hellenistic | The Metropolitan Museum of Art A note: The Greeks were great craftsmen but they also had the proper tools such as the magnifying lenses below: Lenses dated to 6–7th century BCE, on display in the Archaeological Museum of Rhodes. Image credit Login • Instagram The lenses are made of mountain crystal and have a metallic frame with a protrusion, possibly for attaching to some component. On the lens casing, lines likely indicate different degrees of magnification. In Rome, earrings were believed to provide protection against evil spirits and promote good health. Later in Byzantium, earrings were extremely popular and extremely large but they lost their “protective” properties. Byzantine Gold Earrings from Egypt During the Middle Ages in Europe, they lost popularity too due to changing fashions, such as the expectation to cover one's hair with veils or hoods. However, the noble ladies, especially in Spain and Italy, never abandoned them completely. For women in the Renaissance, earrings were seen as a symbol of beauty, wealth, and social status. It would be a crime not to mention the popularity of this piece of jewelry in Asia; in India, China, Japan earrings were also seen as a symbol of status and their designs are stunning: Royal earrings from India, ca. 1st century BCE. https://gr.pinterest.com/pin/48132289738503015/ As I told you from the start, every woman, in every place, in every time period has been fascinated by earrings, they were and still are a universal symbol of status and beauty. Question: What are your thoughts on Yuval Noah Harari's statement, "History isn't just about studying the past; it's the study of change, and it's more relevant now than ever"?
Answer: Learning about history has been, is, and will be relevant. It’s not a coincidence that people have always found a way to keep historical events alive in the collective memory. They used long poems (yes, the epics) before writing was spread, wrote about historical events on a city’s public walls (or even on amphoras!), and storytellers narrated it in the squares. A wise man said some years ago that “the future is written in the past” and he was right as knowing history permits us to trace ηow have we reached this point, the difficulties, the recurring problems (yes, history repeats itself), and the possible solutions that can be used again. The strange thing is that in today's era of information, the study of history, like most humanities, is marginalized. In other words, we are cutting off our roots. If the wise man is correct, then are we perhaps moving towards the end of our civilization? So, yes Mr. Harari, you’re right. What do you do about this? I see nothing but empty words from you.

Question: As prediction engines evolve will our sense of time evolve?

Question: Why did democracy end in Athens?
Answer: It depends on who you ask. A modern-day historian will say the following, more or less. The Athenian democracy, despite that most of you believe the opposite, was restored soon after the end of the Peloponnesian War. It went on until they entered the Corinthian League (the Greek confederation allied against the Persians, in 338/7 BCE under the leadership of the Macedonians). Soon enough, the Macedonians started to intervene in Athenian affairs either by establishing a Macedonian guard in the city or by altering the composition of the assembly, allowing foreigners and servants to participate. A characteristic example is the year 318 BCE in Athens when Philip Arrhidaeus, through his envoys, managed to impose his rule on Athens. He established a new regime and Phocion, the great general of Athens, along with various supporters belonging to the anti-Macedonian party, was arrested and brought to trial at the Theater of Dionysus. From Plutarch: "After Kleitos, (the representative of the Macedonian king), brought them there, he detained them until the authorities summoned the assembly of the people, without prohibiting the participation of anyone, neither slave, nor foreigner, nor citizen who had lost his political rights, but giving everyone access to the platform and the theater. From this, it seems that this was not a real assembly. The direct Athenian democracy never returned to the city. On the other hand, if you could ask an Athenian, he would answer that their democracy lived on, as even in the Roman imperial times, even though Greek cities were located in Roman provinces and governed by Roman governors, nevertheless, they continued to maintain some elements of their autonomy and democratic system. They would be wrong, of course…
